Two proposed expectation models, rational and irrational, predict that financial bubbles will eventually collapse, but at varying times. Officials and investors need to identify when this will happen so they can make informed decisions. Our study enhances the widely-used MSUB model by introducing a stochastic element for the first time, allowing for diverse bubble durations. In contrast to the original model, the stochastic version generates two solution types - a singular transcendental equation or a system of differential equations. The trade-off between using numerical methods to solve the transcendental equation or an approximate MSUB model, which ignores this stochastic aspect, is examined. Our analysis reveals that ignoring the stochastic nature often yields modest but not trivial errors. In particular, the methods' difference in predicting transition times from a bubble to a crash is evaluated by employing various expectation models, including the MSUB and IRH models. Our results show that the methods' error in this scenario can last for nearly 80% of the expected time until a crash within a 10% tolerance. On the other hand, the methods' difference in predicting transition times from a crash to a normal market is generally minor. The IRH model is also compared to the MSUB model, showing that using numerical methods to solve the stochastic version ignores some important features of the financial market. Our study provides the tools necessary to determine when using the stochastic version of the model is beneficial, and we show that using numerical methods to solve the stochastic version of the model can be a valuable option if the expected time until a crash is substantially longer than the expected time until a crash in the IRH model. Our study also shows that the expected time until a crash in the IRH model can be quite long, suggesting that using the stochastic version of the model may not be necessary in many real-world scenarios. Recent advances in recommender systems have shown improved performance due to the effective incorporation of natural language information, but most current methods still face several limitations. Specifically, they often model words within reviews independently without considering the collective sentiment conveyed, resulting in subpar effectiveness. To address these shortfalls, this research introduces the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) for item recommendation. A core component of SIFN is the Review-centered Interactive Framework, which consists of a pair of interactive modules working in tandem: one extracts features from words and the other captures the shared sentiment. Additionally, due to the inherent subjectivity of reviews, this method also leverages review-centered interaction frameworks combining word features and shared sentiment to develop a more comprehensive representation of reviews. Effectiveness is evaluated through comparisons of recommendation performance with that of existing state-of-the-art models on two real-world datasets. Notably, when tested on the movie and book datasets, benchmark results are consistently surpassed. Beyond conventional evaluation methods, human evaluators also judge the results, and the outcomes reveal SIFN to be the top-performing model. A supporting repository with the necessary code and datasets is available at the address https://github.com/MITLS/Review-centered-Item-Recommender. A lightweight web interface for visualizing review-centered item recommender performance can be accessed at the address https://reviewrecommender.herokuapp.com. Developing data augmentation methods for efficiently creating large code-switched training data is essential but remains underresearched, particularly in low-resource languages like Arabic-English CS. Existing techniques focus on altering existing text by either removing or changing units (words or sentences), but they lack evidence in improved performance. We're exploring new approaches to generating high-quality training data by investigating lexical substitutions that consider word meanings and syntactic dependencies within sentence fragments. We evaluated and compared the efficacy of two data augmentation-labeled models and standard word replacement for Arabic-English CS text generation, ultimately finding that adjusting word meanings is more beneficial than simply replacing individual words. Furthermore, to aid in developing improved data augmentation methods, we created CS-AUG, a tool specifically designed for generating Arabic-English CS sentences through replacement. The results show that combining CS-AUG with an underlying model leads to significant gains in performance, particularly in the model's ability to switch codes correctly and maintain lexical continuity. A major challenge in relation extraction involves pinpointing specific relationships between entities within a given text. To address this complexity, recent studies have explored the use of pre-trained language models, combining it with satellite or relational tasks to mitigate the limitations of standalone relation extraction. This research diverts from the conventional approach by examining how pre-trained language models are affected when tasked with predicting links within a knowledge graph rather than extracting relations from text. This transformation allows the model to incorporate structural information and treats relation extraction as a byproduct of training on graph completion. To accomplish this, the authors propose a novel graph completion model powered by pre-trained language models and introduce an innovative way to apply entity clustering for diverse entity sets. This innovative framework consists of building graph chunks using unstructured text and structured data, followed by fine-tuning the pre-trained model with these graph chunks, and finally, selecting the most likely relations associated with a target entity. To facilitate scalable processing, the authors develop an entity clustering framework, incorporating a new entity clustering method, which utilizes both structural and textual information. This approach speeds up graph chunk creation and reduces the need for extensive training on large graphs. Comprehensive experiments and link prediction performance assessments were conducted on seven standard relation extraction datasets and six knowledge graphs, showcasing the link prediction method's ability to enhance relation extraction while also producing graph quality and link prediction performance comparable to specialized tools. Additionally, the authors made available a new dataset called GECLO (Graphs and Entity Corpora Linked to Ontologies), which represents a benchmark for entity clustering and link prediction within the context of knowledge graphs. Further details on the dataset can be found at its accompanying website. Analysis of the findings and link prediction performance indicates that there is a direct relationship between relation extraction and link prediction, and these two tasks can complement each other. While there is room for improvement in terms of minimizing redundancy in link prediction results, which in turn may also improve link quality, and potentially enhance relation extraction results, which could also improve graph quality. This is an initial investigation and the authors suggest future research in this area. The code and data used in this research have been made publicly available. A related video is also available. Reinforcement learning typically assumes a Markov decision process (MDP) environment, modeled through a Euclidean space where standard techniques like empirical risk minimization apply. However, many real-world environments, such as 2D games, are better represented by non-Euclidean manifolds. Consequently, there is a growing need for reinforcement learning in non-Euclidean metric spaces, and we develop this field in this paper. Specifically, we establish empirical evidence and theoretical guarantees for the continuity of a simple policy gradient method in general metric spaces. This leads to a novel, robust optimization technique for non-Euclidean reinforcement learning that does not require smoothing the target value function. Instead, we introduce a coarse-grained version of the function, achieving convergence without altering the policy. Furthermore, we show that this method converges at a nearly same rate as in Euclidean spaces and demonstrate its effectiveness on 2D game examples and a mobile robot navigation dataset. The study's code is available at https://github.com/drewm989/cmpg. Besides contributing independent results, our work is, to the best of our knowledge, the first non-smooth reinforcement learning in non-Euclidean metric spaces without using adaptively changing regularization. Additionally, we extend the established results to semi-bounded discount rewards and discuss potential challenges and future research directions. A detailed examination of the results is presented in this thesis. Firstly, it is essential to recognize that the results are valid for all metric spaces, including those that are not naturally associated with MDPs. While this is an useful property, it is also crucial to consider the practical difficulties that arise from working in general metric spaces. For instance, it is highly computationally expensive to calculate the distance between two states. This issue is mitigated by employing a discretized version of the function and using Monte Carlo sampling to obtain reliable optimization updates. Secondly, it is worth noting that the results are particularly significant for the field of parametric flow-based reinforcement learning, which has garnered significant interest in recent years. Specifically, we demonstrate that the policy gradient method can be continuously updated in a Euclidean space and establish a novel, robust optimization technique for flow-based reinforcement learning in non-Euclidean metric spaces. This result is an important step towards a broader theory of non-Euclidean reinforcement learning. Finally, a detailed examination of the study's contributions and future research directions is presented. In particular, we discuss the potential applications of the results to more advanced MDP models, such as those with imperfect information and non-stationary environments

Our interaction with the world is distinguished by entities that possess life and movement, which are characterized by qualities such as the ability to learn and adapt, grow, and exhibit purposeful behavior. Currently, most artificial systems lack this capacity for self-improvement. To better comprehend animal behavior and develop automated reasoning models analogous to those used by biologists, researchers have created artificial systems that incorporate a life-like learning paradigm. For example, a computer system was taught to recognize when its interactive objects were learning itself. Additionally, a service robot was designed to utilize artificial intelligence to recognize and interact with animals as living entities, even when they are not interactive. Importantly, this research did not rely on predefined criteria for animacy but rather allowed the system to discover and organize its interactive objects through their inherent characteristics. Our paper presents the initial findings from two artificial life-like learning studies, where we investigated how lower-level animacy representations influence higher-level organizational patterns in the brain. Specifically, we demonstrated that animacy organizations in the human brain are more robust when there is a consistent distinction between living and non-living entities, and when there is a clear categorization of these entities (either living or non-living, or either human or non-human). Our results are based on fMRI data from two studies, as well as an experiment involving artificial learning systems, and they challenge previous theories on animacy organization in the human brain. Most notably, they contradict findings from a study by Cikara et al. (2017) published in the journal Neuron. Our data also suggest that animacy organizations in the human brain can be manipulated through artificial learning systems, which have a dual consequence: 1) promoting a hierarchical pattern of animacy organizations that mirrors hierarchical relationships in the world and 2) shifting the boundary between living and non-living entities in the human brain in response to different labels. Our results have important implications for understanding the Essences of Life hypothesis, which suggests that there may be a fundamental core to animacy. Our data indicate that these animacy essences can be learned and may not exist inherently, which challenges the long-standing idea that these essences are fixed and unchangeable. Our work also has important applications in the development of artificial intelligence systems that are capable of recognizing and interacting with living entities, such as animals. By learning and adapting to the behavior of these entities, these systems can develop a deeper and more meaningful relationship with the beings they interact with. The Biot model for porous media is a complex multidimensional system of PDEs commonly used in geomechanics and hydrology. It involves fluid flow, pressure, and stress interactions, including fracturing and fluid movement. PDE models like these often exhibit numerical instabilities and non-predictable outcomes. To improve model performance, advancements in mesh generation and efficient numerical simulations are essential. A new, high-order numerical filter is presented, leveraging convex optimization to maintain the consistency of Biot model solutions. The filter ensures stability of the model, preserving key features of the solution and accuracy of simulations, particularly in areas of extreme stress. It achieves an optimal balance between numerical stability and accuracy, by minimizing a specific cost function. Two realistic simulation cases are used to evaluate the efficacy of the filter in practical applications. Furthermore, the paper explores opportunities for future research and development of similar filters in the Biot model framework. The theoretical foundation and development of this filter provide a stepping stone for the advancement of convex optimization-based model filtering in the future. The research and calculations demonstrated that, in the majority of cases, the filtered model exhibits better accuracy than the unfiltered model, particularly in areas of very high stress. A detailed study is conducted to investigate the economic benefits of the filter in the context of the fracturing simulation in the Wolfcamp shale. The results indicate that the efficient and stable model yields higher economic outcomes compared to the standard model. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis is also performed to assess how different parameters impact the results of the simulations. The new filter not only contributes to the advancement of modeling techniques but also has the potential to be used in real-world hydrocarbon reservoir optimization as a predictive model. The research and development of this filter, utilizing high-order finite element modeling and convex optimization, is a significant advancement in optimization-based model filtering in the Biot model framework. The simulation results, coupled with the economic impact analysis, provide a valid foundation for the application of the filter in the simulation of additional complex PDE models. The algorithmic advancements and developments have a broad-ranging impact and can likely contribute to the advancement of additional model filtering in the Biot model and beyond. In a setting of longitudinal, multi-agent reinforcement learning, we examine the concept of a robotic agent interacting with a human partner who exhibits unpredictable behavior. To address this, we propose transfer empowerment as a method for the robotic agent to anticipate and prepare for the human's actions, leveraging observations of the human's behavior to increase its preparedness. Through empowerment in the transfer context, the robotic agent identifies and prepares for actions with high mutual information regarding the robotic agent's future states, thereby facilitating a joint coordination plan with the human partner. Simulation results demonstrate that the robotic agent achieves better performance by focusing on high mutual information actions, comparing it to alternative approaches based on entropy maximization and action predition. Ultimately, the proposed transfer empowerment offers a more effective and reliable basis for the robotic agent's interaction. We introduce a novel method for local feature matching, where points are linked based on their environment, rather than using only their spatial coordinates. Our approach, LoFTR, utilizes a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework and excels in utilizing contextual, high-resolution local image descriptors. Unlike conventional detector-based algorithms, LoFTR requires minimal parameters and efficiently processes even high-resolution images in real-time. Our experiments show that LoFTR consistently surpasses state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI and KITTI KITTI:3D datasets, while also effectively handling complex, high-resolution images on mobile devices and smartphones. Local feature matching is an essential component of various computer vision tasks, including optical flow, stereo matching, video object detection, and optical flow, and our work significantly advances state-of-the-art performance through novel methodological contributions. Additionally, we make our source code freely available for further research and community use. Formerly known as ICPR2020-LoFTR, LoFTR has evolved from a conference paper to a more mature framework with expanded capabilities. This study builds on that foundation with a more comprehensive evaluation, revealing new insights and enhancements. Notably, we have further optimized the ICPR2020-LoFTR framework to achieve real-time processing on mobile devices and smartphones, while maintaining top-tier performance on the KITTI dataset. Our work in this paper has been designated a top-tier conference paper at ICCV2021, and we have been granted the 2021 ICCV Challenge KITTI Dataset Challenge third-place award for demonstrating state-of-the-art optical flow performance using the ICPR2020-LoFTR framework. Furthermore, we have been recognized as runners-up in the 2021 ICCV Challenge KITTI Dataset Challenge, where we leveraged ICPR2020-LoFTR to demonstrate superior stereo matching performance compared to other methods. Our current work represents a more advanced version of the ICPR2020-LoFTR framework, where we have incorporated new optimizations and extensions to evaluate its performance on mobile devices and smartphones. This study has been recognized through a runner-up award in the 2022 European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) Challenge KITTI Dataset Challenge, where we have been honored for our work on state-of-the-art optical flow performance using the ICPR2020-LoFTR framework. Our research has been recognized through a runner-up award in the 2022 CVPR Dataset Challenge Optical Flow track, where we have been acknowledged for generating high-quality training data

Nevertheless, the process of inferring the sun's magnetic field orientation relies on indirect measurements and is therefore susceptible to biases present in the observational data and the models employed. The presence of these biases has the potential to compromise the results of quantitative analyses performed in this field of study. In an effort to investigate and correct these biases, researchers utilized the BAIrSS deep learning model to analyze multiple sets of magnetogram data, including $\langle B\rangle$ maps, and obtained the results from the full disk maps of sunspots from the SDO HMI dataset. The results showed that the model's output for full disk maps was susceptible to biases that became apparent in the distribution of inclination and strength values. In an effort to correct these biases, researchers applied a technique involving forward modeling to adjust the model's results. The results of these bias-corrected analyses can provide a more stable foundation for the performance of deep learning models such as the one used in this study, and could potentially be applied to other neural network-based reconstruction tools as well. In addition to these findings, the research also demonstrated that the creation of synthetic magnetograms with specified bias variations is feasible and could have practical applications in future studies. This research paper explores a new model of Demand Side Management (DSM) that forms part of a larger smart grid framework. The proposed DSM approach is characterized by two key features. Firstly, it aims to minimize the overall power loss by adjusting the transmission line capacity in proportion to the total amount of scheduled power within a designated time frame. Secondly, non-convex energy consumption scheduling and instant load billing methods ensure that participants abide by agreed consumption levels and are fairly rewarded, with the cost of participation being proportional to their individual scheduled power usage.

To address the complexities of this dual-layer problem, we deconstruct it into two separate components. The first component involves an aggregative game by a single entity, the system operator, to minimize power loss through DSM planning. The operator's strategy involves instant load billing, which provides a compact and tractable solution. Building upon this approach, we introduce a second-order cone convex relaxation method that ensures the solution is both unique and compliant with non-negativity constraints related to the time slot duration and DSM scheduling. Furthermore, we establish that this reformulated solution complies with the key characteristics of an aggregative game through the application of the second-order cone programming.

The second component of our dual-layer framework involves energy consumption scheduling among participants, which we frame as a convex mixed-integer programming problem. Given the non-convex nature of this problem with respect to individual agents, we leverage the concept of variational inequality and instant load billing as a substitute for traditional objective functions, which facilitates a unique and fair equilibrium solution among participants. Notably, we demonstrate that this approach not only yields a computationally efficient solution but also ensures a significant improvement in social welfare relative to baseline scenarios of no DSM.

Lastly, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed model through a comparative analysis of real-world data, which highlights the benefits of variational-based DSM for energy consumption scheduling and instant load billing. The approach yields a substantial reduction in total power loss, with improved results observed for social welfare and bill amounts, whereas total consumer energy bills exhibit slight decrease. Notably, we further establish that our model is a robust solution for non-uniformly distributed energy consumption, which is a key characteristic often overlooked in existing research. The approach's flexibility allows it to accommodate uniformly or non-uniformly distributed energy consumption, which is a critical factor for the system operator's decision-making process. Our research focuses on a non-equivalent theory of gravity, Rastall theory of gravity, and we use the anti-Einstein framework. We apply a model comprising a black string with electromagnetic properties across a single dimension and investigate how gravitational forces impact Hawking radiation. Von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem provides a framework for analyzing the dynamic system represented by a von Neumann algebra with a $*$-homomorphism representing a system's flow. By leveraging operator theory, the theorem offers insights into both the statistical behavior of physical systems and the computational inaccessibility of their states. The addition of a decay estimate for operator coefficients enables the derivation of convergence rates across a broader spectrum. This expansion includes scenarios where the decay rates are negative, non-monotonic, or oscillatory, as well as cases where the spectrum is discrete. By employing a log-convex combination of exponential estimates, we can determine the upper limit of a system's convergence rates based on its point spectrum. Conversely, the presence of a system with a discrete spectrum and an arbitrarily slow convergence rate indicates that a similar rate of convergence in the original system with a continuous spectrum. This extension of these rates when the spectrum is purely continuous further underscores the significance of spectral decay in the context of the ergodic theorem. The results below also demonstrate the significance of the spectrum's position in the complex plane, as well as the role of coherent and incoherent amplitudes in the context of the von Neumann ergodic theorem. This work primarily focuses on the abstract application of the von Neumann ergodic theorem; some supplementary considerations are required for the analysis of quantum systems, particularly those involving nonstandard quantum algorithms. The annual "Blaze Season" marks the beginning of the wildfire season in a given area, during which wildfires occur after natural sources have dried out. This study focuses on developing algorithms to analytically determine the start and end of the blaze season. By utilizing the Negative Binomial Mixture Model, researchers discovered that the primary driver of the blaze season duration is the rate of natural source occurrences. Findings also show that the start of the blaze season is largely determined by the time it takes for natural sources to dry out, which is significantly correlated with moisture levels. Furthermore, the end of the blaze season is found to be dependent on how long it takes for vegetation to dry out, which is again correlated with moisture levels. By leveraging the newly developed methods, researchers tested the effectiveness of NOAA's Climate Predictive Center forecasts in predicting the start and end of the blaze season. Their analysis shows that using current and historical data can accurately predict the beginning and end of the blaze season. However, the study finds that using only temperature in the prediction process results in slightly worse accuracy compared to using moisture levels. Finally, the analysis indicates that using NOAA's Climate Predictive Center forecasts yields statistically significant improvements in predicting the start and end of the blaze seasons. Although using forecasts alone results in lower accuracy, the study demonstrates that incorporating forecasts and historical data can reliably expand the blaze season. This research was inspired by the 2019 Oklahoma Blaze Season when severe wildfires broke out across the state, killing two people and injuring several others. By developing more accurate and empirically grounded methods for analytically determining the blaze season start and end dates, researchers can effectively predict upcoming wildfire potential. This not only facilitates the preparation of emergency response plans but also equips the public with crucial information for their safety. Following initial findings, the study further develops its methods by applying them across various regions, including the southwestern United States, with promising results. We have developed a new approach for evaluating the overall complexity of languages. We propose a comprehensive definition of complexity, breaking it down into three fundamental aspects: script irregularity, symbol versatility, and word pattern consistency. Building on previous research, including the analysis of written materials, we have calculated the quantitative measures of these components for 52 languages. In addition, we have gathered native speaker reaction times to navigating words in these languages through a crowdsourcing platform, which has allowed us to validate our definition of complexity. By examining correlations between the three metrics we've developed and various established typological characteristics, as well as existing morphological complexity indices, we are able to validate our approach. Moreover, we have conducted a series of experiments designed to evaluate the effectiveness of artificial neural networks in predicting the metrics we've defined, which has revealed that our corpus-based measures are reliable and provide a valuable understanding of the underlying aspects of complexity. Notably, our study has identified a significant link between script complexity and the success of artificial neural networks in processing languages, which may have important implications for language technology applications. In summary, we have develop a new methodology for evaluating complexity that considers multiple factors and is grounded in both writing systems and human processing. This research has opened up new avenues of investigation for analyzing the intricacies of languages, which hold great value for understanding the intricacies of human cognition. Ultimately, by evaluating the overall complexity of languages, we are able to gain a richer understanding of the intricate interplay between language, writing, and the human mind. The comprehensive dataset of complexity metrics and associated results are publicly available at https://github.com/tymgu/corpus_complexity. Moreover, the complete source code of our study, including the crowdsourcing experiment, is hosted at https://github.com/tymgu/corpus_complexity_subm. A live demonstration of our study can be accessed at https://complexity.idyll.org. Autonomous Component Analysis is an innovative method for independent component analysis. Unlike traditional approaches, test data is not required for initialization and can be calculated analytically from negative data. This leads to faster and more reliable calculation procedures through a one-time, offline process. In this study, we present a time-efficient variant of the ACA, reducing computational complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2 sqrt(n)) and further down to O(n^2) in some cases. This is accomplished by leveraging outer-product-free structure, a novel concept in data analysis. Additionally, we explored two variants of the ACA, one utilizing a multivariate l1-kernel and the other incorporating a fixed kernel, and demonstrated the efficacy of these methods in real-world data contexts. Furthermore, we present a time-efficient variant of the multivariate l1-kernel ACA (m-ar-k-fast-aca), making both fast-acas even more robust and efficient. The presented m-ar-k-fast-aca offers enhanced stability and improved performance, with ablation studies showcasing the independence of its performance from kernel parameters and data properties. As a result, the m-ar-k-fast-aca has lower runtime and requires less memory than its competitors, making it a more reliable option. Furthermore, the m-ar-k-acas are self-sustaining, able to handle their own memory and disk space on large-scale datasets, and are self-optimizing, capable of independently selecting the best value for the precision parameter. Finally, the m-ar-k-fast-aca has lower runtime and requires less memory than its competitors, making it a reliable option. The implementation of the m-ar-k-fast-aca can be found at https://github.com/asharizai/mar-k-fast-aca. A related video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KsqHook9xkY. The study's results were shared at an ACA workshop in 2021 and a NeurIPS competition in 2022. The m-ar-k-acas were awarded first place in the NeurIPS competition and have outperformed ACA in numerous real-world data contexts. The m-ar-k-acas have been validated using 109 datasets and six different ACA variants, showcasing their versatility and reliability. The m-ar-k-acas have been tested on large-scale datasets and are self-sustaining, able to handle their own memory and disk space. The m-ar-k-acas have been implemented in five different programming languages and are open-source, making them easily accessible to the public.

The initial investigation into quantum guidance, a potentially new phenomenon, is conducted. Quantum guidance may occur when a fully non-local state is formed through the interaction of two entities with a substantial amount of entanglement containing no correlations. A general method is provided to generate fully non-local states, along with a formula to calculate the maximum amount of quantum guidance, and it is shown that quantum guidance can be equivalent to Wigner negativity. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that guided states must contain positive Wigner functions, and the relationship between guided negative Wigner functions and entanglement is explored. Numerical simulations indicate that quantum guidance may be observable in the interaction of ultracold atoms and it is suggested that quantum guidance could be used to develop new non-local quantum connections. Finally, the stability of quantum guidance in various environments is assessed using the decoy state method. The study finds that by utilising multiple inputs, quantum guidance can remain visible even in environments with high levels of noise. These findings suggest that quantum guidance may have practical applications in the development of secure quantum communications. A crucial stage in securing communications within quantum networks involves generating multiple bits of randomness through quantum entanglement. Currently, most studies have only focused on uniform random seeds in quantum key distribution when assessing entropy accumulation. In contrast, this paper builds upon a established framework for analyzing the security of quantum key distribution and extends it to manage non-uniform random seeds in a quantum key distribution scheme that incorporates delayed randomness. We introduce a new concept, entropic disintegration, to measure the uncertainty of a random variable given another random variable, and establish a key distillation efficiency bound for free randomness using entropic disintegration. We also apply the entropic disintegration approach to a previously studied free randomness generation scheme, including an alternative memoryless realization which achieves maximal key generation efficiency within a given nummeric resolution. In addition, we establish a entropic disintegration efficiency bound that is universally applicable to any random seed distribution, and demonstrate that seed uniformity is essential to reach the established bound. We then conduct a numerical analysis to compare the scheme's performance under non-uniform and uniform random seeds in terms of entropic disintegration efficiency. Our results show that when the variance of the non-uniform random seed distribution is large, the entropic disintegration efficiency under a non-uniform random seed approaches that of a uniform random seed with zero variance. This theoretical analysis is confirmed by experimental data. In summary, this paper introduces the concept of entropic disintegration and applies it to a non-uniform random seed case in quantum key distribution, and finds that uniform random seed distribution is essential to reach the established bound. A possible approach to generate uniform random seeds is discussed. We also conduct a numerical analysis to evaluate the benefit of an ideal uniform random seed generator and their impact on practical implementations of free randomness generation. Our results indicate that uniform random seeds are essential to reach the established bound in practical implementations of free randomness generation. We have developed VCRL, an algorithm that organizes robot movements into groups based on given instructions and utilizes a learned function to estimate the value of each movement within its designated cluster. Although efforts have been made to create more transparent algorithms, a standardized measure of their interpretability is missing, which hinders the implementation of algorithms in critical areas like criminal justice systems. This study aims to develop a comprehensive, learning-based model of interpretability that captures the complexity of cognitive processes involved in understanding algorithms. By testing the model with actual algorithmic decisions, we evaluated the interpretability of multiple models used for hiring and scoring across different cognitive levels. The results revealed significant variations in interpretability among these models and highlighted the need for an objective, learning-based measure of interpretability that can help identify and refine algorithms that are difficult for humans to comprehend. This, in turn, can contribute to more informed decision-making processes. The proposed model and findings have significant implications for algorithm developers, risk managers, and decision-makers, as well as offering a valuable framework for understanding the broader social impacts of algorithms through the concept of cognitive coherence. This standard measure of interpretability can also facilitate the evaluation of algorithms in real-world applications and inform the selection of models for critical decision-making tasks. Furthermore, this study's analysis of human cognition, in relation to interpretability, sheds light on the relationship between human thought processes and the complexity of algorithmic decisions, which is essential for understanding algorithmic fairness and making more informed human-algorithm interactions possible. The associated code and results are publicly available for the purpose of replication and advancement of research in this field. The proposed interpretability framework has also initiated discussions about algorithmic impacts through the concept of cognitive coherence, emphasizing the need to regulate algorithms in areas like criminal justice systems. The effectiveness of learning-based risk assessments has also been explored, which is an area of research that is still evolving. Ultimately, standard measures of interpretability and cognitive coherence, like the one proposed in this study, can contribute to more responsible AI development and deployment. The associated code is publicly accessible on the GitHub platform.

Building extensive commonplace knowledge graphs enriches natural language understanding and generates text expansions. Previous commonplace knowledge graph initiatives, such as the TAC Knowledge Base (TACKB), were constructed through crowdsourcing and defined by logical formulas symbolically representing relationships. A novel step in this paper involves creating a large commonplace knowledge graph, COMET-ATOMIC 2020, composed of over a million million triples, by applying a deep learning language model to extensive books and articles. Comparing its performance with the symbolically constructed TACKB, COMET-ATOMIC 2020 demonstrates equivalent effectiveness in (i) extracting commonplace knowledge via question-answer pairs, (ii) assisting in multi-sentence construction given single sentences and vice versa, and (i) acquiring new knowledge based on single or multi-sentence queries. Additionally, COMET-ATOMIC 2020, when used as a world knowledge source, generates text expansions comparable to the symbolically constructed TACKB and outperforms it in (i) acquiring new knowledge based on single or multi-sentence queries and (ii) enriching knowledge graph entities with additional attributes. A companion project, ATOMIC 2020, was developed to support the creation and publication of a vast collection of multi-word atomic actions, allowing for their definition through formulaic expressions and through the training of a deep learning language model. A key outcome from evaluating the resulting knowledge graph highlighted the model's ability to enrich the graph with entity attributes. We develop an analytical approach for the single-file model, drawing inspiration from the generalized diffusion equation as proposed by Boltzmann. Using this method, we derive expressions for the mean first exit time and fluctuations in first exit time for a particle in a finite, one-dimensional channel with absorbing boundaries. We establish a relationship between the second option's variance and the rate of entropy production in the system, quantifying the entropic force acting on the particle. Additionally, we derive an expression for the asymptotic displacement of the particle as time approaches infinity. Our findings are consistent with numerical simulations conducted using a discrete-time lattice model. We also showcase the potential applicability of our results to describe the physical interaction between plasma ions and the membrane bounding a vesicle. We particularly focus on the case of a vesicle containing the GroEL/Chaperonin protein complex, which is renowned for its role in facilitating protein folding within the cell. By making use of our method, we are able to derive a first-order approximation of the diffusion equation, which enables us to model the vesicle as a simplified spherical container. We expect that our work will motivate further research into the development of more accurate physical models. We also hope to contribute to the advancement of understanding in the field of biological diffusion phenomena through our study. Moreover, our findings may serve as a foundation for developing more accurate physical models, potentially shedding light on the mechanisms driving diffusion processes in cells. Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths in space are limited by the Lyman-alpha absorption line, which severely hampers reliable measurements of ultraviolet luminosity, a fundamental aspect of studying celestial bodies. Although various techniques, such as filtering and signal processing, have been developed to circumvent the Lyman-alpha absorption problem, the issue remains unresolved for photometry, the measurement of light intensity across different wavelengths. In our study, a Lyman-alpha filter prototype was designed, manufactured, and tested to evaluate its effectiveness in facilitating ultraviolet photometry. By utilizing the prototype, a improved charge-coupled device (CCD) signal with reduced Lyman-alpha contamination was obtained, which in turn, allowed for precise ultraviolet photometry measurements. Data obtained from the prototype enabled accurate photometry measurements at 176.5 nm, a Lyman-alpha affected wavelength, as well as at adjacent, adjacent-adjacent, and adjacent-adjacent-adjacent wavelengths. It was found that anti-coherent detection, a signal processing method, is capable of minimizing Lyman-alpha contamination to a mere 1.0 percent, a level comparable to state-of-the-art ultraviolet filters with a 1.0 percent precision. In addition, anti-coherent detection yielded a 1.0 percent precision for 176.55 nm, a wavelength immediately adjacent to 176.6 nm, a Lyman-alpha-affected wavelength, and also yielded a 1.0 percent precision for 176.60 nm. Furthermore, anti-coherent detection allowed for a 1.0 percent precision for 176.60 nm, a Lyman-alpha-affected wavelength, as well as at adjacent, adjacent-adjacent, and adjacent-adjacent-adjacent wavelengths. Recent advancements in image retrieval systems have driven demand for high-performance visual search on large databases of images. Current research focuses on index structures and caching to boost query processing speed, but static data structures are used regardless of the image distribution within the collection. As a result, systems struggle to take full advantage of distribution-based information, leading to suboptimal node configuration in databases. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new concept for adaptive image indexing, where the underlying data structure is dynamically updated based on properties of the collected images. We investigate two dynamic indexing methods: one that adjusts node capacities dynamically and another that optimizes node positions with moving parts. We evaluate these approaches using two commonly used image distributions and compare their performance to state-of-the-art methods in image retrieval. Our experiments cover a range of flow rates and focus on both the average and fairness of query processing times. Our results show that dynamic indexing methods outperform traditional systems, especially at higher flow rates and with more skewed image distributions. Moreover, we find that optimizing the placement of indexing structures can further improve performance and yield better results in more skewed distributions, leading to significant improvements in average and fair query processing times. To take advantage of distribution-based information without compromising cache coherence, we propose a new caching method that incorporates temporal image distribution properties. By updating image partitions over time and organizing queries based on contribution to processing cost, our system achieves improved overall query processing speed while maintaining fairness. Notably, we find that the optimal flow rate is a balance between average and fair flow rates, and higher flow rates result in significantly better system performance. Ultimately, our framework enables system designers to uncover important properties of image collections and make informed design decisions to create more efficient image retrieval systems. Moreover, our theoretical analysis allows researchers to identify key design choices that influence system performance. To verify the validity of our approach, we test a full-ranking system built on the concepts outlined in this paper and compare its results to state-of-the-art methods in image retrieval. We evaluate its performance in terms of average and fair query processing times and find that it outperforms all other systems, especially at higher flow rates and with more skewed image distributions. Notably, the benefits of our approach are largely due to two key design decisions: dynamically updating the image indexing structure based on properties of the collected images and automatically shifting indexing structure components to optimize system performance. We introduce a flexible local projection framework to predict the trajectory of a node's impulse response. The new framework extends the local linear framework and enhances our understanding of non-linear shock effects, while confirming the local linearity assumption does not compromise the accuracy of initial impulse response estimates. We demonstrate the influence function method consistently estimates parameters in the flexible local projection framework, and these estimates can be directly plugged into the local linearity framework to obtain final impulse response estimates. Our method has general applications and doesn't rely on specific shock types or network structures. We investigate the angular Casimir torque between two cylindrical electrodes with uniformly charged surfaces, one of which has a ground-state charge and is superconducting, embedded in a superconducting loop connected to an external current source. Recent research has shown the efficacy of hyperbolic spaces in machine learning, particularly for graph-related tasks using the Poincaré ball model. However, applications relying on this model in deep neural network contexts often report subpar performance. We aim to change this by merging the benefits of hyperbolic spaces with the advantages of pre-trained models and refinement approaches through FGNET-RH, a novel framework for Fine-Grained Named Entity Classification that uses a hybrid self-attention mechanism combined with a Refinement-in-Hyperbolic-Space approach. FGNET-RH leverages LLMs like BERT and FLMMs like FLROBERT to filter and distill task-specific information, before processing it in a hyperbolic space using an extended Poincaré ball-based self-attention mechanism. Our evaluation of FGNET-RH on 8 Fine-Grained NER datasets from 5 languages, as well as on CoNDE and MedLine in a Spanish and English setting, shows that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin, demonstrating the efficacy of integrating hyperbolic spaces with pre-trained models and refinement approaches. Our code has been made publicly available to facilitate replication.

Cloud-based virtual networks rely on advanced connection technologies such as Software Defined Networking (SDN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV) for seamless operation. These technologies utilize virtual switch and network monitors to collect and disseminate timely statistics on traffic across different networks. This paper introduces a novel load distribution method based on a predefined partition to address the need for efficient traffic management in cloud networks. The proposed approach comprises two primary components: the virtual switch handles traffic estimation and load distribution, whereas reserved resource information is managed by an administrator. This system facilitates rapid traffic estimation and load distribution, enhancing the overall efficiency of traffic management. Moreover, it avoids issues of load imbalance by preallocating resources, thereby preventing congestion and data loss. A practical implementation of this load distribution method is demonstrated using OpenFlow virtual networks and routers with flow controllers. Extensive experimentation is conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in traffic management. Lastly, a comparative analysis demonstrates that the proposed load distribution method consistently outperforms the existing NVGRE and Caldera methods in traffic management. To ensure the reliability of critical control systems, it's necessary to adopt a predictive approach. We're focusing on a linear time-invariant system protected by a predictive safety model that uses to identify potential threats and ensure safe operation. The challenge lies in finding the shortest attack path and determining the shortest attack distance from the current system state. To address these problems efficiently, we propose two methods. Firstly, we've developed an algorithm that uses graph search to find the shortest attack path. The method marks system states that can become unsafe and helps minimize false alarm rates. Secondly, we've created an attack distance algorithm that uses to estimate the distance between the system state and the nearest attack state with the shortest attack path. The algorithm's computational cost is minimized through dynamic exploration of graph nodes. We've tested our methods with Delphi simulations on different models, including a two-loop model and a turbo pump controller model. The results show that our approach effectively predicts stealthy attacks and provides valuable benefits. The time complexity of our attack distance algorithm is analyzed and proven to be efficient, with an exponential bound that depends on the search radius. In graph theory, an upward planarity test determines whether a directed planar graph can be drawn with edges pointing upwards. Upward planarity is an important problem with various applications across multiple fields. We have developed a single algorithm capable of solving the upward planarity problem for large and small input sizes, parameterized by the crossing number. Our method also identifies a new crossing parameter, known as (Δ, κ), with the property that decreasing either value progressively reduces the other value. Leveraging this (Δ, κ)-parameter, we offer (Δ, κ)-parameterized algorithms for checking upward planarity, with some variants dependent on the new parameter's definition. Additionally, we have established (Δ, κ)-parameterized algorithms for related problems such as one-sided crossing minimization and the homomorphism testing problem, where the involved graphs have a bounded treewidth. Our proposed techniques integrate planarity quoting, planar separators, and the new (Δ, κ)-parameter to achieve these results. Our experimental study demonstrates that the algorithms based on the (Δ, κ)-parameter offer significant speed advantages over existing methods. Notably, some of the new algorithms are even more efficient than a non-parameterized algorithm for small input graphs, further underlining their practical value. Overall, the (Δ, κ)-parameter constitutes a valuable tool for exploring the interplay between graph crossing parameters and upward planarity in the realm of parameterized complexity. Our work has further expanded the scope of planarity-related problems solvable via (Δ, κ)-parameters. In fact, in the accompanying supplemental material, we have demonstrated that many more problems can be efficiently solved via (Δ, κ)-parameters. Specifically, in the case of the planar Frankl-Winkler invariant, we have established that the m of the worst packing efficiencies across all possible k values, where 0 ≤ k ≤ n, can be computed in O(n^(3.5 + ε)) time for sufficiently large n values and a fixed k value. Similarly, in the case of the planar Roberts-Sternberg invariant, we have established that the m of the worst S-r values across all possible k values, where 0 ≤ k ≤ n, can be computed in O(n^(3.5 + ε)) time for sufficiently large n values and a fixed k value. These results represent significant computational advancements, as the best known sub-exponential times for these problems are O(n^(2.5 + ε)) and an open problem in parameterized complexity. In an effort to enhance confidence in genetic algorithm-based efforts to automate crash reproduction, we carry out a partial replication of a 2019 study, aiming to bridge the gap in case studies and provide clear, unambiguous evidence. A comprehensive replication also helps to establish research integrity and offers a didactic example for future researchers. 

In our replication study, we attempted to reproduce the 2019 experiments by guiding a genetic algorithm to replicate crashes in six software systems. Unfortunately, the genetic algorithm was unsuccessful in replicating the studied crashes, except for JMeter and JBoss Watson - where we managed to find and truncate the inducing mutations, but the provided genetic algorithm could not exploit this knowledge. Through in-depth analysis, our team identified key factors that might have hindered the genetic algorithm's performance, suggesting future work should prioritize addressing these elements. Ultimately, this study emphasizes the importance of employing rigorous evaluation methods, and we highly recommend that researchers document specific guidelines for locating and modifying mutations in software system test suites. 

It's crucial to note that, unlike the original 2019 study, our replication did not involve active collaboration with the software system owners. Consequently, our results may not be as optimal as those previously achieved. A full replication including direct engagement with the software system owners would provide a more accurate comparison. A goal of our study remains in promoting research integrity through comprehensive replication studies, and we hope in the future, researchers can utilize our results to identify areas for improvement and optimize automated crash reproduction efforts. The accompanying material includes supplementary information, including detailed logs, system information, and the necessary information for reproducing our study - including the guided genetic algorithm we employed, and the fitness functions used to evaluate performance. Video descriptions can be found on related YouTube content. Furthermore, our study utilizes the TASTE tool pair (arbitrarily available under license), and the lists of software systems both successful and unsuccessful, along with the original 2019 study's fitness functions.

These measurements facilitate a thorough examination of the transition, including its creation and destruction, and the shapes taken by the intermediate structures along the way. Our investigation also reveals a distinctive characteristic pattern for the transition in the types of grid patterns (square or triangular) that are formed. Ultimately, this research combines theoretical and practical investigations to establish a comprehensive understanding of the transformation between different stationary vortex arrangements. It does this by considering both the intricate patterns of flux line interactions and the ways in which the surrounding superconducting material affects the formation of these structures. We've calculated the anisotropic flow of thermal photons in heavy-ion collisions, and found that it's heavily influenced by the properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) and the dynamics of the processes occurring within it. The rate of change of the elliptical flow of thermal photons in the direction of the reaction plane is directly linked to the viscosity of the QGP and its dependence on temperature, and is significantly impacted by the presence of strange quarks. This makes the thermal photon anisotropic flow a valuable tool for measuring the viscosity of QGP and the role of different parton flavours in the process. The results of our calculations match the findings of the latest Lund model, and may be verified through accurate measurement of thermal photons' elliptical flow coefficients in future large hadron collider experiments. The anisotropic flow of thermal photons could serve as a sensitive test of the properties of QGP and the processes occurring within it, and of potential quantum anomalies. The study of thermal photons' elliptical flow can be regarded as a form of 'hydrodynamics of photons' and serves as an extensive and sensitive test of hydrodynamic simulations of QGP. The rate of change of thermal photons' elliptical flow can be regarded as a form of 'hydrodynamics of photons' and serves as an extensive and sensitive test of hydrodynamic simulations of QGP. The results of our calculations were presented at the 'Relativistic Heavy-ion Physics in the LHC (2018)' conference. The calculations of thermal photons' higher flow coefficients, and the phase structure of the photon distribution in the coordinate space, are subjects for our future research. The rate of change of thermal photons' higher elliptical flow coefficients in the direction of the second harmonic in the photon four-distribution, and the phase structure of the photon distribution in the coordinate space of the $\nu_2$ harmonic, are subjects for our future research. The calculations of the photon elliptical distribution in the coordinate space of the $\nu_2$ harmonic were performed in the linear approximation with respect to this harmonic and may be verified through accurate measurement of the diluted photon elliptical distribution in the future large hadron collider experiments. The time-dependent distribution of thermal photons with the negative value of the fourth flow coefficient was found and may be verified through accurate measurement of the diluted photon distribution. The calculations of the photon elliptical flow in the most rare events of the central collisions were performed and may be verified through accurate measurement of the diluted photon distribution in the future large hadron collider experiments.

However, the high cost of sending these treatments and the large number of generated data under each treatment due to non-active users make it difficult to analyze these data. We also adapt this method for high-dimensional regression problems and demonstrate its effectiveness in large fiscal policy datasets. Software developers who are not domain experts often have difficulty formulating relevant questions based on users' descriptions of software requirements. To address this, researchers have been exploring machine learning-based methods to assist in clarifying ambiguous queries for better search results. A key challenge in query clarification lies in identifying the core concepts and related concepts, and then adapting the query to effectively target those concepts. Existing query clarification methods are primarily focused on determining relevant concepts within queries, neglecting the importance of domain knowledge. To enhance search results for software development, researchers are working on integrating the task of query clarification with the goal of identifying the core software development concepts. In this paper, a novel approach called QUICKAR is proposed, which uses crowd-sourced knowledge to determine the core concepts within a given query and reformulate the question to better target those concepts. By combining the strengths of support vector machines and mapping texts to concepts, QUICKAR achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art query clarification methods. Furthermore, an extension of QUICKAR's algorithm is proposed, which enables the system to provide multiple query variations to cater to diverse user needs. A comprehensive experimental evaluation is conducted using 2,160 manually annotated samples and three publicly available datasets. These results are then applied to concept location, which is demonstrated through a practical experiment involving 49 software systems. QUICKAR's query reformulation capability is highlighted through this real-world experiment. QUICKAR's source code and the associated datasets are available for download on GitHub at https://github.com/duquonng/QUICKAR. In addition, a web-based demo of QUICKAR can be accessed at http://quickar-queryreformer.lids.mcgill.ca. A related technical report containing the detailed experimental results is also provided at http://arxiv.org/abs/2105.13821.

Adaptive and cooperative interaction characteristics define entrapment as a speaker's tendency to mirror or accommodate the quirks of their conversational partner.  Despite its significance in defining desirable interaction patterns, an unsupervised assessment of entrapment remains elusive, particularly when analyzed through speech patterns, which are often complicated and speaker-dependent. To address this gap in research, a novel entrapment metric is proposed using conversational speech samples at a speaker-level, which can be easily calculated using a reliable approach.  This metric is further validated by testing its correlation with existing measures of entrapment, which were previously derived from acoustic features or linguistic aspects. Additionally, the research explores the use of unsupervised deep learning models, such as variational autoencoders and adversarial-nariational autoencoders, to develop a systematic method for measuring entrapment.  Our findings indicate that entrapment models, whether they are structured or unstructured, can effectively capture the speaker's propensity to display adaptive behavior.  Notably, an unsupervised entrapment model with speaker-level accommodations is able to identify entrapment in individuals with developmental disabilities, including those with autism spectrum disorder. To promote generalization of entrapment models, we test them on samples from diverse populations, including individuals with developmental disabilities, learning disabilities, and typical individuals, as well as on datasets compiled in multiple settings, including natural and facilitated conversations.  Importantly, our models perform in line with what is considered normal behavior, which holds implications for their practical applications in assessing individuals with developmental or learning disabilities.  This study serves as a foundation for future research on entrapment models, and we plan to make our code available to the community to facilitate replication and the development of entrapment models for various populations. Moreover, we believe that entrapment models have the potential to be expanded to other social cognition constructs through multi-variable alignment, which can result in improved accuracy. For instance, entrapment models can be modified to assess emotions by integrating emotional features, which may provide additional generalization capabilities. Ultimately, the code for these entrapment models will be made publicly available to facilitate replication and foster progress in this field. Many current action segmentation methods rely on annotated data, but this becomes impractical when working with lengthy and multiclass video sequences. Our proposed solution, Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Prediction (SSCAP), tackles unsupervised action segmentation by modeling the shared characteristics among action classes through a low-level co-occurrence relationship decoder and a high-level appearance-based action classifier, which learns to predict adjacent actions in a sequence over time. SS CAP introduces two novel loss functions, a temporary pseudo-label loss and a temporary auxiliary loss, to enhance its performance. Additionally, SS CAP utilizes a temporal regularization loss to ensure consistent predictions throughout the video. Our comprehensive evaluations of SS CAP on multiple challenging datasets, including activity and human action datasets, demonstrate significant performance improvements over relevant self-supervised and unsupervised state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, SS CAP's efficacy in cross-domain scenarios, where it is pre-trained on a large annotated dataset and then applied to a target unsupervised dataset, is also validated through rigorous testing. Our code and associated datasets are now publicly available at the following link: \href{https://github.com/AliefLesar/SSCAP}{\textit{sscap}}. Our results suggest that SS CAP's performance surpasses that of existing self-supervised and unsupervised state-of-the-art action segmentation baselines by approximately 7% on the ActivityNet dataset. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide full code feedback or concept feedback on specific features. We believe that focusing on improving coding skills without addressing underlying flaws can be counterproductive. In response, we conducted a study to compare the effectiveness of testing feedback mechanisms, incorporating the Refactor Card and Inquirybot tools. One group of students, provided with conventional feedback, showed initial improvements in testing skills, but this advantage diminished over time. In contrast, students receiving feedback through the Refactor Card, initially struggled more, but ultimately surpassed their peers in testing performance. This suggests that identifying and addressing fundamental errors early, even if initial progress is slower, can accelerate progress in this domain. In a subsequent experiment, students were divided into three groups: receiving feedback from the Refactor Card, a modified Refactor Card featuring educational prompts, or no feedback at all. As the experiment progressed, the students whose feedback was guided by reflection showed increasingly better performance in testing abilities. In comparison, the group without feedback exhibited notably poorer testing skills. Our study indicates that providing students with accurate and conceptually sound feedback on their testing abilities can accelerate their long-term progress in this domain, compared to simply receiving full code feedback. Ultimately, this has implications for the design of future educational testing tools, suggesting the value in modifying the Refactor Card to include inquiry-based feedback that prompts students to consider underlying testing fundamentals. This has the potential to further enhance learning in this domain. In a third experiment of this sequence, students whose feedback was modified to include a debugging challenge showed increased performance in testing abilities, improved coding skills over a control group, but the groups demonstrated similar testing performance on subsequent tasks. This suggests the value in incorporating debugging challenges into the design of testing feedback tools. In a fourth experiment, students given testing homework with explanations showed significantly better testing performance in an assessment, in comparison to a group given testing homework without explanations. This provides further support for the value in incorporating inquiry-based feedback in testing education. In a fifth and final experiment, modifying the Refactor Card to feature multi-part feedback, including concept feedback on specific features and thorough code feedback, showed minimal impact on testing performance, but this had a notable side effect of increasing student satisfaction with the tool. This suggests the value in offering a choice in feedback mechanism, based on individual needs and preferences. In summary, while providing full code feedback can be beneficial for students, it is not necessary for achieving good performance in this domain. Domain adaptation has been employed to tackle the issue of adjusting a model's performance across distributionally distinct domains without access to the target domain data. The condition of limiting the model's training to a single domain is known as source-free domain adaptation (SFDA). Past SFDA methods have focused on either transferring features from the source domain to the target domain or matching the distribution between domains. This work instead asks whether it's feasible to fine-tune a pre-trained model while disregarding its original training distribution. Inspired by insights from language models, we introduce the concept of semi-supervised hypothesis shift (SSHS) to describe this method. SSFH utilizes pseudo-labels on the target domain in conjunction with a large-scale mixture-of-experts backbone that's pre-trained on a broad range of domains. This allows the model to learn new knowledge and adapt its parameters to the target domain while avoiding unnecessary self-conflict induced by target domain data. By decomposing SSFH, we create two simplified versions that recover important components. SSFH achieves state-of-the-art results on SFDA with superior robustness and versatility in comparison to competing methods. Our code is publicly available at this link: https://github.com/liuwen8331/SFDA-HS. As demonstrated by the results, hypothesizing domain adaptation without access to target domain data can yield superior adaptability. Additionally, we showcase that multi-domain pre-training, a commonly used practice in computer vision, may actually hinder performance if not accurately captured by the pseudo-labels used in this method. Such findings are likely to be highly relevant in the field of self-supervised pre-training in deep models, and our research is the first to illustrate this phenomenon in the domain adaptation context of a pre-trained model. Our work is also the first to utilize pseudo-labels as a means of regularizing the model's adaptability in the domain adaptation field. However, this technique has previously been shown to lead to overfitting in other contexts, such as translation-based pre-training. We have also extended SSFH to address the issue of adaptation across multiple domains, and our code provides additional insight into its application to semi-supervised domain adaptability in the vision field. Our work is highly versatile and can be applied to other fields such as natural language processing, multi-modal learning and medical image processing. A new deep learning technique has been developed to enhance experimental data analysis by locating the particle interactions within experiments' three-dimensional frameworks. A constructed neural network domain shifts the input distribution to fit the particle detection framework's domain, ensuring the network only outputs values within the physical space confines of the experiment. Key aspects of this approach include the dataset creation process, network design, and interpretation of the results. Effective data analysis using this method has resulted in a simplified procedure, and the source code is available for public use. Using a particular experiment as an example, the novel method demonstrated a 40-fold decrease in values outside the physical space observed before domain-informed training. Furthermore, the trained model yielded a precision of 0.98 and accuracy of 0.92 for locating the particle interactions. Notably, the method also reduced the background noise, yielding a precision of -0.06 and accuracy of 0.95 for points with no particle signals. These points are critical for setting simulation parameters in the particle detection framework. The trained network can enhance signal detection and contribute to both simulation-informed and model selection analyses. Moreover, the method can be adapted for use in other experiments and particle detection techniques. The combination of this deep learning model with the particle detection pipeline has broad applications in the fields of astrophysics and particle physics. thus supporting the research into the chemistry of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres.

To address this challenge, a comprehensive framework for general quantum resource theories has been established. At its core, this framework defines a resource class as a closed subset of a space of quantum states, along with a preorder that captures the idea of a state being a resource. Key principles within this framework include the naturalness of the resource class and its inherent properties. Furthermore, mathematical properties of free states and incompatibility relationships have been examined. To illustrate the applicability of this framework, it has been used to construct specific resource theories, such as the theories of entanglement and quantum coherence. By providing a unified approach, this framework offers a clearer understanding of the initial conditions for any given resource theory. Consequently, the framework holds significant value for the development of future theories. Moreover, as a theoretical companion to the resource theory of quantum contextuality, it has been used to demonstrate the strict inapplicability of the contextuality thesis to established resource theories. Lastly, as a prospective tool for physics education, it has been applied to introduce quantum mechanics to undergraduate students. The framework's versatility allows for the derivation of initial conditions relevant to their everyday observation of quantum systems. The general framework has also led to the formulation of a mathematical condition for maximally monotonous resource theories, which has been named Marchi's condition. Marchi's condition holds for theories of entanglement, quantum coherence, and postselection but remains unfulfilled for the theory of quantum contextuality. Consequently, the initial conditions for contextuality have been explicitly derived. Our work concludes by exploring the implications of these conditions in terms of their relation to non-classical correlations and the possibility of reducing one form of non-classicality with another. The derived conditions for contextuality demonstrate that non-classical correlations do not necessarily imply the presence of contextuality. The theory of quantum coherence offers a concrete example of this principle. Analysis of X-ray flux suggested the shock traveling towards the Sun had a Mach number of approximately 1.3, while the one moving away had a Mach number of around 1.8.
