Light field technology is currently a focal point of research for reversible video compression, as it has the potential to restore original video data while reducing storage requirements. However, commercial video codecs still fall short of enabling practical reversible compression of high-resolution videos. Our solution to this problem is a new learning-based compression method, consisting of an efficient capture network and a practical compression network. The capture network generates a reduced number of sub-aperture images from the original video, while the compression network uses these images to predict the full sub-aperture images of the video. A unique paradigm called 'parallax-aware modeling' is utilized in the prediction process, which accounts for the spatial displacement of camera views and temporal coherence within the video. Our experiment results show that our approach matches the quality of state-of-the-art light field video synthesis methods, while achieving comparable compression efficiency as the state-of-the-art light field compression methods. Our finding also shows that the compression efficiency of our method can be further improved by incorporating it with existing video codecs. For example, when our method is integrated with the LP4C codec, it is possible to achieve up to 40% additional compression ratio compared to using the LP4C alone. As a whole, our framework has the potential to greatly enhance the compression efficiency of future light field video codecs. Our framework can be utilized as a bridge between still image compression codecs and the emerging reversible light field video codecs like LP4C, enabling the deployment of these codecs on devices capable of capturing high-resolution light field videos. Achieving effective cross-lingual information retrieval using vector embeddings is possible without any additional supervision besides monolingual data.  However, when applying pre-trained monolingual models in a cross-lingual setting, a critical limitation becomes apparent: the inability to positively sample similar items, as they belong to different languages.  In response, we explore the use of interactive models, which can translate or encode pairs of language-specific vectors into a shared multilingual space.  While they overcome the previous challenge, they still require processing pairs of language-specific vectors at query time, which hampers their potential for parallel training and efficient caching.  To resolve these issues, we develop two enhancements: training a non-interactive model with a parallel dictionary and incorporating a dictionary for lookup in order to obtain a initial cross-lingual embedding for a query.  By doing so, we surpass the existing benchmark in cross-lingual information retrieval and demonstrate substantial parallel training and caching gains with an accurate, low-dimensional representation of data. Population health research, including low and middle income countries, heavily relies on health surveys like the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS). A key requirement for surveillance is estimating population health outcomes in small areas with sufficient precision. Given limited resources, such countries often struggle to conduct the extensive surveys needed for small area estimation, prompting the use of design-efficient techniques and realistic statistical models. This research compares the performance of two design-based approaches, using simulated DHS datasets. We analyze the fit of two statistical models, both Bayesian and conventional, and explore the efficiency of two design-based strategies: pooling samples from adjacent areas and concentrating cases in areas of high response rates. Our results show that pooling and sampling in favorable areas are effective strategies, offering significant gains in estimation precision. Furthermore, our analysis reveals modest improvements when using a realistic model instead of a nominal model, and we recommend combining these strategies with modern modeling techniques to enhance small area estimation in resources constrained settings. 

Key words: Small Area Estimation, Low and Middle Income Countries, Survey Design, Bayesian Models, Random Effects.

This paper introduces a novel multi-period non-linear time series model inspired by sparse Bayesian learning. The inherent challenges in multi-period modeling are the lack of exogenous variables and coherent dynamics between different time periods, making prediction from one period to the next highly reliant on previous data. We tackle this issue by developing a forward-looking prediction approach within a Bayesian framework, using a structured sparsity-promoting prior to select the most relevant information from past data for prediction in subsequent periods. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding sparse multi-period predictions, accurately mimicking the true underlying structure of the time series, and surpassing performance of single-period models both in predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. The time series modeling approach is exemplified through the analysis of the US auto industry's sales data. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/wangyong121/mbf_net. Object Detection, a fundamental computer vision task, has gained significant attention from the community. While advancements have been made in closing the gap between machine and human performance on detection tasks, a major limitation still exists in the form of limited training data for detection. Various methods have been tried to address this issue, including the use of weak supervisions. Yet, state-of-the-art object detection networks remain sensitive to training data variability. In this work, we propose a different type of weak supervision - pseudo bounding-box labels. By providing broad area annotations without precise boundary definition, these labels can effectively train modern convolutional networks. We also develop a simple algorithm that generates such pseudo labels at a fast pace. Our extensive evaluations show that pseudo bounding-box labels yield significantly better results on three benchmark datasets compared to other available methods. Moreover, we introduce an open vocabulary detection benchmark, the Oxford Object Dataset, aiming to promote research on zero-shot and few-shot learning for object detection. Our code will be publicly available.

A study was conducted to explore the ionized, atomic, and photo-disassociated gas surrounding the R Ophiuchus star, S1, located within the nearby Rho Ophiuchus cloud. This cloud is situated approximately 125-175 parsecs from Earth. To understand the complex structure of the region, we analyzed data from radio telescopes, observing molecules such as NH3, H2O, and HCO+. We also utilized data from radio receivers that measure emissions from ionized hydrogen gas, in addition to data from photodissociation region (PDR) models and tracers like C18O. Our analysis revealed gas with distinct properties within the north-western area of the region. A proposed model of the region suggests that a compact PDR is positioned almost exactly between two expanding photodissociation regions that are pressuring gas into a concave shape towards the inner PDR. This PDR is thought to be the result of gas pushing past the S1 wind column. Gas in the region exhibits characteristics consistent with either being ionized or atomic, with ammonia autoconversion providing an explanation for this property. However, this interpretation is not exhaustive and a more detailed analysis of the region's energy balance, in addition to additional data from higher angular and temporal resolution, is required to further our understanding. As such, we plan to utilize the Giant Millimeter Wave Telescope in China for a more nuanced analysis in the future. This research utilizes a unique combination of tracers to explore the region, in particular a unique study of NH3 in the region which may have implications for a broader understanding of similar regions within the inner PDR. A follow-up observation is planned to confirm these initial results. Furthermore, we propose a model to explain why there may be asymmetry in the region, suggesting that a potential PDR is being pinched by gas from the north-east. This model is thought to be the result of gas dynamics from a proto-planetary nebula that is interacting with the cloud. This interpretation has implications for a broader understanding of similar regions within the Milky Way and nearby star-forming regions. The notion of veracity in data refers to its reliability or accuracy. Semantic technologies and knowledge graphs are particularly sensitive to veracity issues, which are becoming increasingly common due to the rising volume of distributed, web-based data sources. The development of open, community-driven knowledge graphs like DBpedia, YAGO, and Wikidata has been pivotal in creating a global knowledge base (KB). However, veracity concerns have arisen due to the diverse crowd-sourced contributions and information aggregation from multiple sources. The lack of sophisticated validation methods and plagiarism detection tools in KBs, coupled with the limited availability of veracity assessment techniques, makes it necessary to address veracity aspects in KBs. This paper offers an comprehensive overview of recent advancements in veracity assessment, highlighting its key aspects, techniques, and tool implementations, as well as identifying areas for further research and development. The paper also explores the application of transformer models in veracity assessment through a transformer-based approach to detect plagiarism and evaluating veracity in KBs, demonstrating the superiority of transformer models in this context. The primary outcomes of this study are a comprehensive review of veracity in KBs, an in-depth analysis of relevant techniques, and a transformer-based approach to veracity assessment. The secondary outcome is a new dataset for evaluating state-of-the-art methods in veracity assessment, such as finding the most similar paragraphs and detecting plagiarism. The code and related plugins are available on GitHub for the dataset, plagiarism detection, and KB veracity assessment. The goal is to motivate the community to develop more sophisticated veracity assessment techniques grounded in transformer models, which have the potential to significantly benefit the semantic technology and KB communities. The paper also aims to inspire future research and development in this area. The final outcome is a publicly available video presentation of this study. The conclusion provides a comprehensive review of the primary study contributions: a thorough overview of veracity assessment, a transformer-based approach to veracity assessment that outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods, and a new dataset for veracity assessment. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is a highly resource-intensive task but some studies have found that it often involves selecting architectures that could have been identified through less expensive methods. In order to mitigate this problem, we conducted an in-depth investigation into the time complexity of NAS, focusing on the relationship between time and budget constraints. The results revealed that current results are likely skewed towards smaller budgets due to excessive interference between architectures, which was confirmed by our finding that the performance of NAS is greatly impaired when using a large dataset such as ImageNet, whereas the Cell-level NAS performed up on par with expert-designed models when using a smaller dataset such as CIFAR-10. In order to reduce interference, we developed a new NAS technique called PathNAS which incorporates path length as a constraint to avoid cross-architecture interference, resulting in improved results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with an ensemble model. A lottery ticket is a versatile ticket that can be used in multiple ways, 
such as in lotteries, raffles, or other types of games and promotions. 
Although often viewed negatively, this ticket can be a lucrative way to 
generate income if purchased strategically. In our study, we develop a method 
to calculate the predicted earnings from a lottery ticket based on the 
probability of winning and the value of each win. By incorporating time and 
market trends into our formula, we can predict the optimal time to purchase a 
ticket, and the best way to maximize the predicted profit is to buy tickets 
early in the morning or late at night when the market is less active, as this 
limits the ability to adjust the ticket price based on market conditions. 
Additionally, we provide guidance on how to effectively sell lottery 
tickets to maximize the predicted profit. Our findings are empirically tested 
using actual data from a popular online platform. Overall, our approach 
reveals that purchasing and selling lottery tickets can be a highly profitable 
investment if the right strategies are employed. In particular, we found that 
the predicted profit from our method averages $78.96, which far exceeds the 
expected loss often associated with lottery tickets. In fact, the expected loss 
from traditional lottery purchases is approximately -$0.10. Therefore, our method 
offers a game-changing approach for investing in lottery tickets and can help 
generate significant profits if the recommended guidelines are strictly 
followed. Our study bridges the gap between financial economics and machine 
learning by applying AI technology to predict the earnings from purchasing 
lottery tickets based on market trends and using data-driven analysis to 
calculate the predicted value of each win, which is crucial for making 
informative investment decisions. In the future, we plan to expand our research 
to explore additional investment opportunities beyond purchasing and selling 
lottery tickets, which could lead to equally lucrative outcomes. In particular, 
we intend to make modifications to our formula to predict the predicted value 
of wins based on the actual outcome of previous wins, which would enable us to 
optimize investment decisions at a more granular level, which could result in 
even greater returns. In the near future, we hope to successfully defend our 
innovative investment strategies in the form of a doctoral dissertation.  In 
addition, we would like to express our gratitude to Mr. Tomar for his selfless 
support and for allowing us to use the data from his online platform at 
www.lotteryaash

The VisDA 2022 challenge aims to investigate whether models can effectively generalize to unseen domains. The 2022 challenge features a diverse dataset with 15 training domains and a test domain, drawing from the COCO dataset. The task involves training a model using domain-specific data from 15 training sets and adapting it to the test domain with minimal supervision. The visdav20 dataset, a preprocessed version of the COCO dataset, serves as the benchmark for the challenge. A. Rajpurkar et al.'s submission, "Uncertainty-aware Domain Adaptation for VisDA 2022," obtained the top rank in both tracks of the challenge. The submission involves two auxiliary components: (1) domain-disentanglement, using a variant of the DINO self-supervised learning algorithm, and (2) uncertainty-calibration, using a variant of the FIT framework. The combination of these components yields state-of-the-art performance on the visdav20 dataset. The submission is based on the code from NeurIPS 2022 challenge entries "Dino: Self-supervised Visual Representation Learning" (#5) and "Fit: Fault-tolerant Imaginary Label Transfer," which provide the domain-disentanglement and uncertainty-calibration components respectively. The submission is prepared by A. Rajpurkar et al. (Bell Labs, IBM Research). The results show that the uncertainty-aware approach yields performance gains in both classification and segmentation tasks, with results improving by over 3% on the visdav20 dataset relative to the previous state-of-the-art. The submission details can be accessed via the challenge website at https://visda2022.chalearn.org/submission/149/. The submission code and demo can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/rajpurkar/vqanet_baselines/tree/visda2022. The corresponding project page is available at https://bell-labs.com/rajpurkar/visda2022. The authors thank the Bell Labs, IBM Research, and IBM AI Research for their support. A new, spherical version of t-SNE has been developed to address this issue by modeling spherical data with a von Mises-Fisher distribution and optimizing its parameters through a mirror descent-based maximization of the t-SNE's original gradient in a spherical context. We've modified the Diagrammatic Monte Carlo technique to account for the self-energy operator in two-dimensional systems with complex interactions. This update allows us to preserve an exact bosonic spectrum in the energy denominator of the self-energy diagram. Our results show that in the two-dimensional Fermi gas, a small amount of attractive interaction at half-filling creates a polaron with a non-zero life time, even at absolute zero temperature, despite expectations of a diverging life time in one-dimensional and zero-range three-dimensional systems. Additionally, we found that the self-energy in the weak interaction limit matches the established variational solution. Furthermore, by analyzing the imaginary self-energy part, we established a critical interaction strength separating the weak and strong interaction areas with a polaronic state. This interaction strength, approximately 0.036 times the Fermi energy, is notably larger than the critical interaction for Fermi liquid quasiparticles in three-dimensional space and one dimension, indicating a more stable quasiparticle in two-dimensional systems. By removing the conservations associated with the self-energy diagrams through a sum over the cut diagrams, we discovered that the Diagrammatic Monte Carlo results can be described by a simple formula relating the polaron life time to the interaction strength for small interaction strengths. This result was verified by matching the Diagrammatic Monte Carlo life time with a Monte Carlo simulation in two-dimensional systems. This method for calculating the self-energy in two-dimensional systems extends the applicability of Diagrammatic Monte Carlo to systems with a varying interaction strength, and it also allows for a life time calculation for other quasiparticles in two-dimensional systems. Further details on this method and its application to two-dimensional systems for various types of interactions and fillings can be found in two related papers. One paper investigates the nature of bound states near a critical temperature for repulsive interactions, and the other paper examines the life time of quasiparticles in two-dimensional systems with repulsive interactions. Further details on these methods for calculating the self-energy in two-dimensional systems can be found in two related doctoral theses. One thesis focuses on a two-dimensional system, and the other thesis focuses on a three-dimensional system with a varying interaction strength for repulsive and attractive forces. Diagrammatic Monte Carlo was also used in systems with a varying interaction strength for repulsive forces in three-dimensional systems with standing waves and three-dimensional systems with ferromagnetic spin-exchange interactions. This work led to the discovery of superfluidity in three-dimensional systems with spin-exchange interactions and a life time for quasiparticles

This research focuses on developing persistent homology of color assignments (chromatic structures) in order to capture their topological properties. It introduces a concept called persistent homology of colored graphs through alpha structures, which can represent graphs in various contexts. Building on the alpha structure framework, we define a hierarchical system of chromatic structures indexed by values, extending the existing framework. By demonstrating that these structures form a chain in a category, where morphisms are transformations that preserve the graph's topology, we establish the framework's validity. Furthermore, we show that this chain has the property of "unique left limits" and can be treated as a simplicial object within a particular space. Based on the alpha structure framework, we define a hierarchical version of persistent homology of chromatic assignments, which captures the evolution of graphs' topological properties over time. The proposed theory is then applied to examine the persistent homology of colored networks in biology. Specifically, we analyze coexpression networks of cancer disease types, investigating the topological properties of individual genes across different networks. By applying the theory, we identify genes with the most significant persistent homology values, suggesting their involvement in central biological processes and higher-order interactions. This approach can serve as a tool for evaluating complex high-dimensional interactions in biology. The research also includes theoretical discussions on the extension of the alpha structure framework to more complex graph representations like multi-colored networks, as well as general chromatic assignments. However, these topics require additional mathematical modifications, which are explored in another paper. Finally, the related code has been made available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/kayac/bio_persistent_homology.

Optimality conditions are implemented via a new mathematical tool called the P-Algebra, which is developed in a companion publication. It's revealed that the difference between the GDoF achieved with optimal and binary power control is at least $\frac{\sqrt{K}}{3}-\frac{K}{6}$ and at most $2\sqrt{K}-K$, which establishes an upper and lower extremal bound that together prove a prior conjecture stating the difference between the two controls is at least some constant greater than zero for $K$-user networks. It's shown that the value of this constant is directly related to $\sqrt{K}$. This work also includes an analysis of possible network topologies that may yield an extremal GDoF outcome, specifically, linear, triangular, tetrahedral, and tetrahedron-based networks, which provide an extremal GDoF basis for $K$-user networks. In the context of IoT, data is constantly generated and analyzed in real-time to provide feedback to users. Categorization is a crucial process used in real-time systems, particularly in IoT and surveillance areas. This paper focuses on the process of categorization in IoT, discussing the challenges it poses during the auditing stage and proposing a formal framework for understanding and creating categorization models. By integrating formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shfer theory, this framework offers a universal language to represent and adapt these models according to specific criteria, such as security constraints and transaction policies. Additionally, the framework provides a method to balance categorization models with uncertainty in IoT systems, mitigating the effects of data uncertainty while maintaining the system's security and privacy. An illustrative case study demonstrates the practical application of this framework in an IoT setting. Furthermore, this paper outlines a procedure for auditing and adjusting categorization models in response to changing system requirements. Using formal methods ensures that the system remains secure and compliant with relevant regulations, such as GDPR. Lastly, this paper provides a perspective on future research directions related to categorization in IoT systems. As an supplementary resource, we are providing the source code of the categorization audit tool so that our findings can be verified and built upon by other researchers. These systems include colloidal gels that are formed from a highly concentrated suspension of particles. In this study, a new method was developed to manipulate and characterize the mechanical properties of these gels by using high-intensity vibrations. This process, known as "rheo-acoustic gels," involved introducing ultrasonic waves into the gels and measuring their dynamic behavior under various conditions. The study showed that by introducing these vibrations, the particles in the gel could become temporarily disordered and cause the gel to transition into a more liquid-like state, reducing its mechanical strength and allowing it to be easily deformed. Additionally, the gel's ability to flow was measured as it was subjected to different levels of shear stress and vibration frequency. The findings revealed that the gel's flow behavior could be affected in two distinct ways, known as "yielding" and "flow," which are typically associated with liquids. However, even in the "flow" state, the gel's mechanical strength was found to be maintained due to the vibrations. This research provides new insights into the behavior of soft glasses and opens up new possibilities for tuning the flow and mechanical properties of these systems using external vibrations. The study also introduces a new characterization method that can reveal hidden aspects of a gel's behavior that cannot be accessed through conventional methods. The framework of "rheo-acoustic gels" may lead to the development of advanced materials that can adapt and change their properties in response to different external vibrations. The potential applications of this idea could extend to various fields, such as biomedical, aerospace, and engineering. The Collatz Conjecture, also known as the 3x+1 Problem, is a mathematical hypothesis that has withstood all efforts to disprove it thus far, despite over eighty years of attempts. This simple-seeming conjecture concerns a sequence of numbers starting with a positive integer $n_0$, which is governed by a specific transformation rule ($3x+1$ if the number is odd, $3x+2$ if the number is even). A key claim of the conjecture is that regardless of the initial value $n_0$, this sequence of numbers must eventually reach zero. This article will provide a comprehensive overview of the conjecture, examining its history, theoretical foundations, and notable results, as well as highlighting some of the many open questions surrounding this enduring puzzle. Furthermore, the article will share some insights from an authorial perspective, highlighting potential avenues of research meritworthy of exploration. Ultimately, the article will offer a reflection on the significance of the Collatz Conjecture and the broader $\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{NP}$ problem in the realm of modern computing and mathematical theory. This essay is intended for an interdisciplinary audience, with the goal of inspiring younger researchers and seasoned professionals to delve deeper into this fascinating topic. A related GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/barakmichal/Collatz-Conjecture. This study reveals that stability can be achieved by having agents only offer their top choice, provided that agents are strategic in choosing proposals and agents are aware of this limited choice mechanism.

In the model used for this research, agents rank potential partners without implying any preference for one over another, except for their top choice. This ranking is called a 'weak preference order'. It's found that a mechanism where agents only ask their top choice partner to be matched, with the option to decline, yields the most efficient set of matches when in common preference order is known. Current automatic assessment methods for summary quality are limited by their static nature, relying on manually defined features and principles that don't accurately capture the subtle aspects of human judgment. Human feedback is valuable for teaching AI systems, but existing supervision methods are imperfect, leading to summaries that may lack coherence or fidelity to the original text. We aim to develop more practical and versatile solution by leveraging large-scale human feedback to train a more effective assessment metric utilizing advanced language models. Our proposal, SummScore, assesses summary quality by measuring the degree to which it resembles a fine-tuned language model's preference, thereby providing real-time evaluation and remediation of summaries. We demonstrate SummScore's efficacy in evaluating non-neural, neural, and transformer-based summaries, as well as its potential to automate the creation of dataset annotations and yield more accurate rankings of summaries in various genres and domains. Additionally, SummScore can be applied in various practical contexts, such as detecting and correcting inaccurate automated summaries, enhancing the quality of human-generated summaries, and identifying the most relevant portions of low-quality summaries. We have released SummScore along with relevant resources (data and code) for further research and development. Ultimately, our work marks a significant step towards creating a transferable understanding of summary quality assessment, thereby facilitating the development of more sophisticated automated tools in the field of summary evaluation. From a mathematical standpoint, we have developed a fresh framework for making accurate predictions. This framework draws upon the idea that a measured signal can be precisely restored using a limited number of linear equations, as long as the signal's frequency spectrum has sufficient density. This concept builds upon the findings of Tain and Janssen in 2017. This study also examines the scenario in which instead of using regular linear equations, quadratic measurements are employed. When applied to a range of traditional and naturally occurring signals featuring logarithmic or log-periodic frequency spectra, our research demonstrates that the use of quadratic equations allows for accurate recovery with a significantly reduced number of measurements. The problem of autonomous driving requires integrating vast amounts of sensory data from various sources to generate meaningful representations.  Beam-Transfer-ReRepeat (BEVFusion) is an efficient and effective framework that fuses the data from LiDAR and cameras to generate high-quality level 2-4 beam features.  By leveraging lightweight and adaptable beam features and precise sensor timing alignment,  BEVFusion provides superior performance compared to traditional self-supervised auto-encoders and achieves state-of-the-art results in autonomous driving. 

We evaluate the efficacy of BEVFusion on three challenging scene understanding benchmarks:  Car make and model classification on the COCO dataset,  Semantic segmentation on the KITTI dataset,  and  Semantic instance segmentation on the nuScenes dataset.  Furthermore,  we showcase the framework's capability to generate high-quality 3D visual features which demonstrate value in other autonomous driving applications such as control, localization, detection and tracking. 

Across the three benchmark tests,  BEVFusion achieves exceptional accuracy with notable statistics:  It achieves a remarkable 77.1% mean average precision (mAP) on the COCO dataset,  achieves state-of-the-art performance with 82.9% mAP on the KITTI dataset,  and  achieves state-of-the-art performance with 51.1% mAP on the nuScenes dataset.  The simplicity, efficiency, and effectiveness of the framework, along with the flexibility to incorporate it into a variety of autonomous driving applications, make it suitable for widespread adoption.  A demonstration video is also available at:  https://youtu.be/YC3Bml5w5.  The code and 3D beam features are now readily available on the GitHub repository:  https://github.com/asharakeh/BEVFusion.  And finally, a related docker deployment framework is also available on GitHub:  https://github.com/asharakeh/BEVFusion/deploy. This impact causes a distortion that may result in the occurrence of intricate, non-linear laser-induced diffraction patterns. These patterns can take on various forms such as sinusoidal modulation, bragg-like reflections and even ring-like patterns, and are often attributed to dynamic changes along the laser propagation path. However, a comprehensive understanding of the thermal profiles and their effects requires precise numerical simulations that take into account the interplay of laser absorption, thermal conductivity and heat dissipation. These calculations have often been simplified, assuming the liquid's absorption to be uniform and neglecting higher order temperature gradients. However, we have recently conducted more rigorous simulations that incorporate spatial variations of absorption and consider the full range of fourier components involved. Our simulations accurately capture the experimental observations previously reported, and reveal the complex interplay of temperature gradients and molecular dissipation that gives rise to the observed spectral content. This study provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for the interpretation of the diffraction patterns produced when a liquid is heated by a laser, and will serve as a starting point for the exploration of non-linear laser-induced processes. An experimental case study involving Amazon sales datasets and graphical models for evaluating pipeline efficiency was conducted, which showed the effectiveness of our approach in supporting big-stream analytics. Our work highlights the value of incorporating a hybrid query planner in big-stream analytics pipelines. We investigate a subset of problems associated with weighted iterative graph normalization, focusing on fundamental properties and efficient solutions. Unlike conventional methods that demand the graph's underlying structure, we explore two key variants without this requirement. Our first variant involves finding the maximum weight independent set in a graph where each node's weight is determined by the minimum of its original and the average of its neighbors' weights in an iteratively normalized graph. For this, we offer two efficient solutions. Our second variant involves identifying the best independent set in a graph optimized through iterative normalization, given a predetermined candidate set. For this, we present a specialized solution tailored to specific graph types. Our theoretical findings, such as bounds on the maximum weight independent set in naturally occurring graph sets, and in random 3x3 matrices, also include an analysis of the independence number in a specific type of graph known as the hypercube, as well as the proof that a particular problem is NP-complete. Our experiments, encompassing real-world and synthetic datasets, also demonstrate the effect of different graph types on the independence number's behavior. Our code, which can be accessed at https://github.com/jayakrushnani/normalization, is now publicly available for use. Recent discoveries of magnetically active stars emitting X-rays and radio waves have sparked renewed interest in their radio emission. Focusing on flare star binaries, this paper aims to understand the origin of persistent low-frequency radio waves, possibly resulting from magnetospheric electron-cyclotron-maser-emission (ECME) in their surrounding atmospheres. Utilizing recent observations from the long-baseline low-frequency array, we analyzed CR Draconis, a binary system consisting of two late-type stars, providing daily observations over 157 days and 13.5 hours of continuous coverage. Our findings include frequent low-frequency radio waves, seasonal variations in intensity, and a strong correlation with the brighter component of the system, potentially due to a magnetically dominant star. By following CR Draconis in its orbital cycle, we confirmed prior X-ray observations and found radio waves on nearly 50% of the monitored days during their periastron phase, when enhanced coronal activity is expected. Moreover, we observed low-frequency emission and X-rays independently of each other in the periastron phase but not in the apastron phase, indicating a complex atmosphere influenced by magnetic fields. Moreover, we found CR Draconis to be one of the sources with the longest-lasting radio waves, lasting up to 98 days in a continuous state. Our study indicates that the magnetic interaction between the components of the binary system likely contributes to this phenomenon, possibly due to DC currents driven by non-thermal electrons. The origin of these particles, however, remains unclear and requires further investigation. Nonetheless, we offer two potential explanations for the observed radio waves, specifically the possibility of non-thermal electrons appearing in the magnetically linked atmospheres of magnetically active binary stars during their periastron interactions. Alternatively, we also consider the possibility of non-thermal electrons in the magnetospheres of planets, resulting from comet impacts, as an additional potential explanation for the observed low-frequency emission. While this hypothesis remains highly speculative, it is consistent with the observed radio waves in the Centaurus-Rho system, which shares similarities with the CR Draconis atmosphere. Moreover, we provide evidence that supports the ongoing activity of the cometary tail from RS Ophiuchi in 2013, which resulted in non-thermal electrons in the magnetospheres of the planets Saturn and Jupiter. Consequently, we propose the possibility that non-thermal electrons in the magnetospheres of planets in the Centaurus-Rho system could lead to the emission of low-frequency radio waves, as observed in CR Dra

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets composed of loosely connected three-spin clusters. Specifically, we investigated the thermodynamic behavior of a strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and the previously proposed triangle-square lattice model, which were both proposed as potential models for superconducting SrCu(Po4)6. Our results include the thermodynamic data, the specific heat, entropy, susceptibility, and the magnetic order parameter, obtained at finite temperatures and in the zero-temperature limit. These results were also compared with existing findings derived from analytical and numerical solutions, along with an examination of the numerical convergence of the trimer-cluster approach and its scalability for future research. Moreover, we discuss how the observed properties of the strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and the triangle-square lattice model align with those proposed by the quantum Monte Carlo simulations presented in P. Fouquet et al., New J. Chem. 44, 15764 (2020). Specifically, we investigate how the deeply gapped states of the strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and SrCu(Po4))6 facilitate the emergence of near-degeneracy between the gapped and gapless states at the quantum critical point of the triangle-square lattice model, which is characterized by opposing sublattice frustrations. These findings are supported by the observation of near-ideal quantized specific heat and entropy distributions that add qualitative evidence to explain the superconductivity observed in SrCu(Po4))6. Our approach is also adaptable for use in investigating the thermodynamic behavior of additional two-dimensional quantum cluster systems. Recently, pre-trained language models have demonstrated the capability to perform zero-shot learning when equipped with classification prompts.  Unfortunately, developing these prompts proves to be a time-consuming task, largely due to the lack of clear principles guiding the creation of prompts.  To address this, our research shifts the focus from manually crafting prompts to automatically generating them based on datasets.  By treating prompt assemblies (the input requirements for a model to make a prediction) and datasets as interconnected entities, we explore strategies for fitting pre-trained models to make predictions based on these assemblies.  Through this process, our model, which we call a Meta-Tuner, can produce optimal prompts for any given dataset, enabling it to perform zero-shot learning.  Our findings indicate that our method can learn cross-domain zero-shot learning representations and outperform existing techniques in various benchmark tests.  Furthermore, we discovered that the prompts produced by our method can also be applied in few-shot learning scenarios, proving to be highly versatile.  To provide a deeper understanding, our research includes a comprehensive analysis of the inner workings of prompt-based learning, aiming to establish clearer principles for the creation of these prompts, which could ultimately lead to significant reductions in the time and effort required to develop these prompts in real-world applications.  We publicly disseminate all of our code and datasets at https://github.com/sgsyu/prompt-learning.  Lastly, our research delves into the potential drawbacks of using pre-existing classification prompts, highlighting certain limitations associated with the usage of these prompts in prompt-based learning.  To advance the state-of-the-art in this topic, our method can be extended to automatically generate datasets as well, which could further enhance the utility of prompt-based learning and lead to the development of the first fully-automated machine learning framework that does not require any labels. We introduce novel spectroscopic redshift algorithms for identifying reliable optical and submillimeter redshifts based on far-infrared and submillimeter data. These algorithms generate far-infrared and submillimeter light curves by modeling dust-obscured radiation from star-forming regions, using a Bayesian approach with a MIRCHA code implementation. For nearby ultraviolet sources with minimal dust influence, our algorithm effectively simulates far-infrared and submillimeter light patterns that accurately reflect their redshifted counterparts. Therefore, for objects without time-varying or irregular star-forming activity, their far-infrared and submillimeter light curves can uniquely determine their optical or submillimeter redshifts. Based on this principle, our work develops comprehensive diagnostic tools: a far-infrared and submillimeter redshift predictor and a far-infrared and submillimeter redshift tester. By employing a predictor, we estimate likely redshift ranges for an object. Using a tester, we validate whether detected near-infrared or submillimeter emission from an object corresponds to its true redshift. Together, our instruments, dubbed High-z Sudoku, help ensure the precise determination of redshifts and identify robust optical and submillimeter redshifts for future follow-up observations, especially those related to gravitational wave transients and magnified and unlensed distant galaxies. We also describe how our tools can be adapted for first-time spectroscopic redshift measurements, as in the case of the Extremely Red K7 source, for which we estimate a redshift range of 1-5.2, suggesting the possibility of a z ~ 2 starburst galaxy hosting a luminous radiation source at its center. Finally, we outline the future enhancements needed for our spectroscopic redshift diagnostics to reach the far edge of the universe, particularly in the context of the CO(5-4) emission line redshift diagnostic and millimeter and submillimeter line detection in the redshift range of 6 and above. This research uses large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations to study the dynamics of a model Heisenberg system with unit spins on a triangular lattice. The model is particularly interesting because its ground state can be traced back to three distinct order parameters: N\'eel antiferromagnet, collinear antiferromagnet, and a state known as a chiral spiral. Our findings show that the third state has a significant influence on the dynamics, especially near the points where three ground states intersect. Additionally, we discovered new response signals in the dynamics that indicate the breaking of these orders and explored their connections to other spin liquids, especially the notorious `quantum critical point' in materials like YNi2O3^5. Experiments have previously struggled to find this critical point, and our model suggests one possible reason: the difficulty in identifying it through static measurements, and in the presence of specific symmetry-breaking transitions, where the dynamics and scaling of certain properties are not uniform. Our study used lattice calculations to explore the phase transition in SU(3) Higgs theory across a wide range of temperatures, replicating and deepening prior findings that the critical temperature for the phase transition varies based on the Wilson flow criterion. We discovered that an analogous variation in the Josephson coupling also exists, depending on the criterion, but only at a certain threshold. Furthermore, our computations revealed that the complex phase of quark masses induced by the imaginary part of the Yukawa interaction has a significant impact on holonomy and results in a distinct phase transition when coupled with Wilson flow. In contrast, the variation in the critical temperatures based on different Wilson criterion applications is either non-existent or, at high flows, diminishes for fictitious quark masses. However, the variation is reinstated at a higher regime. We propose a different phase based on these distinct critical temperatures, which we call a deconfinement regime. Conversely, the shift in the critical temperatures is less pronounced in the case of real quark masses. In line with standard definitions, we identified a distinct confinement regime below a certain threshold and a deconfinement regime above it. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that pseudoscalar meson correlation lengths are the lowest in SU(3) Higgs theories with real quark masses. Moreover, our computational results indicate that the shift from confinement to deconfinement regimes, as well as standard scales, diminishes as the number of flavors increases. Interestingly, the standard scales show a similar trend but with a slightly greater slope. Lastly, our study discovered that the pseudoscalar meson correlation lengths are the lowest in SU(3) Higgs theories with real quark masses and standard scales, but the shift from confinement to deconfinement regimes, as well as standard scales, decreases with increasing flavors. Cr$_2$Al, with a tetragonal $I4/mcm$ crystal structure and a space group of $D_{4h}^{12}$, is part of a family known as the Cr$_2$T$_2$ compounds, which exhibit antiferromagnetic properties at an unexpectedly high temperature of around 300 K. This, combined with its $I4/mcm$ structure, presents challenges in determining the in-plane magnetic arrangement and exchange interactions. Using neutron diffraction, the magnetic structure of Cr$_2$Al was studied, revealing a magnetic arrangement that follows a type-II antiferromagnetic pattern. This arrangement is characterized by the sharing of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic bonds in a plane, with the latter being the dominant interaction. By employing the analysis of neutron rocking curves and computational modeling, the exchange interactions were found to be primarily influenced by the long-range spiral order, resulting in a second-order magnetic transition at $T_N = 300$ K. This unique set of exchange interactions explains how Cr$_2$Al achieves its ability to antiferromagnetic properties at a high temperature. This study provides valuable insights into the magnetic behavior of Cr$_2$Al and other Cr$_2$T$_2$ compounds with similarities in their crystal structure. Furthermore, the research also highlights the potential drawbacks of using conventional techniques to study magnetic structures, with the corresponding suggestions for future magnetic structure analysis. Lastly, the findings of this study have significant implications for the understanding of materials that exhibit magnetocaloric effect and Weyl semimetal properties. By reviewing the literature, it was discovered that only Cr$_2$Al and V$_2$O$_5$ possess large entropy changes and critical temperatures, making them promising candidates for the application of magnetic refrigeration; meanwhile, other compounds are characterized by small entropy changes and/or critical temperatures, failing to exhibit the magnetocaloric effect. A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $
u$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, thereby incorporating essential features of the collision operator that emerge through its bilinear form. A numerical investigation reveals that the $
u$-model outperforms a conventional kinetic model based on the hard-sphere intermolecular potential, particularly in boundary layer simulations. Additionally, the $
u$-model is capable of reproducing the adaptable-velocity collision frequency observed in the Shakhov model with greater accuracy. Nonetheless, the $
u$-model's success is confined to simulations of slip and blowup problems, where the velocity distribution function's shape differences between the $
u$-model and the Shakhov model become minimal; in more complex weakly rarefied flow simulations, where accurate velocity distributions are required, a more advanced model with a more sophisticated velocity-dependent collision frequency might be necessary. Furthermore, the $
u$-model's performance, similar to that of the Shakhov model, is hindered by its inability to accurately simulate boundary conditions at the wall, an issue that needs to be addressed through a higher-order approximation of the collision operator in order to produce physically meaningful results. Ultimately, the $
u$-model serves as an effective kinetic model for simple kinetic simulations, but its potential extensions are limited by its inability to capture higher-order collision operator dynamics. A more advanced iterative solution to the collision operator, one that is informed by additional thermodynamic properties, could potentially lead to a higher-order kinetic model capable of accurately modeling velocity distributions and corresponding macroscopic flow behaviors. Moreover, the $
u$-model's success, similar to that of the Shakhov model and other velocity-dependent kinetic models, relies on a synthetic relaxation time approximation of the collision frequency; in order to model collision frequencies informed by actual potential theory calculations, a more complex thermalization model based on an iterative solution to the collision operator might be necessary. Nonetheless, the $
u$-model serves as an valuable stepping stone for advancing from Boltzmann's collision operator to more advanced kinetic models. Furthermore, although this investigation was confined to rarefied monatomic gases, the model's potential extensions are not limited to these systems; in particular, incorporating quantum effects into these gases could lead to the discovery of novel quantum phenomena waiting to be described by more advanced thermalization models. Natural Language Processing tasks typically rely on large datasets, but a novel approach aims to create more authentic language models by tapping into less structured, real-world data and avoiding pre-cleaned inputs. Implementing this goal in practical terms means developing a model that can independently understand and process language without relying on human interpretation. A key challenge lies in training such a model, especially since human explanations often strayed from their core purpose during tasks. A recent model, called the Universal Transformer, claims to capture the underlying meaning of language, but it was trained on 180,000 questions accompanied by human explanations. In contrast, this research aims to demonstrate the feasibility of training a semantic interpreter with significantly less data, using a technique inspired by biologics. Specifically, the method leverages word embeddings, forms local co-occurrence networks, and integrates them into a model called RETRO, which can be efficiently applied to various tasks, including question answering. Ultimately, the proposed approach enables a language model to surpass human-level understanding with remarkably little training – merely 50-100 labeled examples. Despite this remarkable efficiency, the model still makes occasional mistakes rooted in word ambiguities, providing valuable avenues for future research. Unlike traditional language models, RETRO's performance scales poorly with the complexity of a task but excels at handling low-quality inputs, providing promising foundations for naturalizing language interpretation in cutting-edge AI applications. Researchers at Fermilab are developing advanced silicon sensors for the Electron-Ion Collider's forward region.  Three sensor technologies - fully 3D, high-temperature superconductor, and low-loss diamond - are being explored for the outermost tracking system at an electron-ion collider.  These sensors' integration with fast, custom digital circuits could enable in-real-time charge clustering, reducing data transfer rates and minimizing dependence on high-rate conditions.  A comprehensive study is being conducted to evaluate this hybrid system's feasibility, including testing and developing complete sensor modules.  Such a hybrid system could enhance precision and reduce data transfer rates for the EIC, potentially increasing the rate at which scientists can process information.  A demonstration module featuring a 3D sensor and complete readout electronics has been built and tested in a high-radiation environment to assess its capabilities.  This project aims to create multiple fully-functional sensor systems by the end of 2022.  These innovative sensors' advancements will not only benefit the EIC but also other experiments, including those at LHC, J-PARC, and SHiP.  A cutting-edge semiconductor device is also being developed, integrating the sensor and digital circuits into a single, complex system, which has also been successfully tested in a high-radiation environment.  This new device's integration of functions will reduce data transfer rates, decrease power consumption, and lower the overall cost of the system, potentially increasing the rate at which scientists can process information.  A batch of these advanced sensors is scheduled for delivery in 2023.  Researchers are also developing a high-speed and efficient data transfer system, a precision measurement system, and a data analysis method to utilize the advanced sensors' capabilities during experiments.  A new experimental setup, including the ALICE TPC's inner detector, a detector at the LHC Luminosity 2023, and the SHiP experiment, is being utilized to test the advanced sensors' performance in real-world conditions.  Results from these tests, including the delivery of the new data transfer system's first production, have been obtained.  Researchers are also studying the advanced sensors' magnetic properties, including the magnetic moment of a detector's main frame, and the effects of various radiation on the sensors and their performance in real-world conditions.  A detailed study is being conducted to evaluate the sensors' precision and their potential to increase the rate at which scientists can process information, with the goal of delivering the first complete hybrid system to the EIC by the end of 2022

Although this approach is typically applied to gamma-ray bursts, it has shown promising results for AGN light curves, leading to the discovery of hidden 'flares' in XMMU J0142+2003. A re-examination using the X-Ray Spectral State (XSS) method revealed two states, with the second possibly indicating an ejecting outflow that was previously considered alternative explanations for the light curve. A breakdown of the light curves into energy bands revealed flares in the hard band, with the soft band showing little variability except at the second state. To explain the light curve, two models can be considered: models of jets failing (quinariation) or of jets being launched (flares/jets), however, with the current data, it is not possible to distinguish between these two possibilities. Regardless of the explanation, the light curve indicates that the source of the variability is at the jet base rather than further downstream. This discovery could potentially be used to constrain jet evolution models and support the hypothesis of relativistic jets existing across the whole mass spectrum of AGN black holes including low mass and UV-AGN. Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) through two different methods: one that measures the 21 cm line's luminosity and another based on a 23 GHz frequency slice sensitivity. These measurements show SFRs 3-4 times higher than those derived from 24 μm Spitzer data, yet comparable to those from 24 μm and UV data. Comparing our H30α and UV observations, we found the galaxy exhibits a significant scalability of its SFR, much like that of the Milky Way. This shows the H30α and UV relationships are both stable and correlated with the galaxy's stellar mass. Furthermore, the H30α and UV relationships are both sensitive to a galaxy's metallicity, the H30α more so, which suggests the role of photon density in governing the formation of stars and planets in these processes. Finally, the H30α and UV relationships are both sensitive to a galaxy's metal enrichment, the H30α more so, which can be utilized as a means of detecting populations of dormant stars. These can be differentiated from active stars and planets through the application of the Sobolev decoupling technique. This distinction is possible because the active stars and planets in these galaxies have substantially lower abundance and produce less heavy element mass in their present form than would be expected for such low metallicity galaxies. Yet, the active stars and planets may eventually lead to such an effect as they age and burn more of their initial mass in the future. Conversely, the active stars and planets may also lead to a reduction in the formation of future stars and planets if they indeed follow in the path of the dead, inactive remnants as has been observed in the low metallicity galaxy IC10. This effect can be prevented, however, if the initial enrichment in heavy elements is not very great and the initial abundance of hydrogen is not very far from its optimal range for star and planet formation. If the decoupling of these spectral lines can be confirmed, the decoupling mechanism itself can be confirmed and the Scalability of SFR measured from the H30α and UV frequencies can be confirmed. This would then suggest the photodissociation of H2 can occur more easily in the low metallicity galaxies than in the high metallicity galaxies and the decoupling of these frequencies can occur more easily in the low metallicity galaxies than in the high metallicity galaxies

Conditional expectation operators are a fundamental concept in modern mathematical probability and are extensively employed in various applications across statistics, signal processing, and quantum information theory. This thesis addresses the issue of estimating a conditional expectation operator without making any assumptions about its structure, utilizing data from observations. Specifically, it focuses on establishing strong consistency for the empirical conditional expectation operator based on sample data, and demonstrates that this estimator is adaptive in the sense that its performance exhibits optimal robustness when the underlying conditional expectation operator is known. Furthermore, this result is shown to be applicable in a variety of contexts by proving that the empirical conditional expectation operator is not only strongly consistent but also differentiable and smooth. An application of these findings is provided in the form of a efficient method for estimating entanglement-breaking operators used in various quantum information processing tasks. Additionally, this research delves into the estimation of conditional expectation operators in two types of quantum systems: discrete and continuous. While the underlying principles are similar, our analysis encounters significant obstacles due to the infinite-dimensional nature of the problem, which is characterized by pathological phenomena such as functional difficulties, complex mathematical structures, and the absence of probabilistic tools, all of which distinct from the familiar one-dimensional case. To address these challenges, we develop novel tools, including new functional inequalities and novel probabilistic methods that contribute to generalizing established probabilistic techniques to multi-dimensional settings. This research culminates in a comprehensive study of the asymptotic properties of empirical conditional expectation operators in continuous systems, involving intricate mathematical arguments and requiring the utilization of diverse techniques from the fields of operator theory, probability, and functional analysis. Lastly, we briefly outline a range of influential questions that remain unanswered in this area and encourage future research in these directions. Through this work, we aim to make a significant contribution to the literature on operator estimation theory, which has previously been largely focused on one-dimensional settings, thereby opening up novel avenues for research in the multi-dimensional case. The methods and findings presented in this thesis are anticipated to be broadly applicable not only within the fields of quantum information theory but also in various other contexts, including statistics, signal processing, and machine learning. Furthermore, this research is anticipated to foster future research in the area of multi-dimensional operator estimation and related fields. The challenge of estimating relationships between entities or resources in knowledge bases has received relatively little attention from machine learning communities despite the widespread adoption of static models. This research addresses the link prediction issue in knowledge graphs that change over time by developing an approach combining both static and temporal models. A novel multi-task network architecture leverages static models to generate initial predictions, which are then refined by adjusting entity embeddings based on temporal information from time-stamped triples in the graph. Experimental validation across three datasets demonstrates that our method surpasses state-of-the-art temporal and static models in link prediction. A comparative analysis of development and evaluation results sheds light on the generalization capabilities of static models and suggests that, to some extent, results can be transferred across datasets. However, working with high-energy pulses comes with challenges, particularly in the areas of beam degradation, heat buildup, and mechanical instability. This problem not only affects the pulse quality but also the long-term stability of the oscillator. In this study, we explore the issue of heat-induced beam distortion and examine methods to minimize its impact by incorporating a curved or multi-bend fiber tail to the conventional ring cavity configuration. We demonstrate that the flexibility offered by curved fibers in multi-bend configurations provides numerous options to manage the beam size while maintaining a small spot size at the mirror interface. We also utilize fast numerical simulations to model the nonlinear interaction within the fiber and analyze the resulting frequency spectra in the presence of ring-down losses. This investigation leads to the discovery of an optimal balance between high pulse energy and narrow frequency spectra, which we believe will facilitate the creation of high-quality, stable mode-locked oscillators with low chirp. Our results and insights can be applied in the development of compact, high-repetition-rate oscillators with the potential to deliver over 100 mJ of pulse energy at 1 MHz repetition rate, significantly advancing the capabilities in ultrafast laser technology. We have developed an innovative framework for federated learning, the Resource-Conscious Asynchronous Online federated learning (RCO-FedOnline) algorithm, designed to tackle nonlinear regression tasks efficiently, despite the presence of uneven data and unequal computational resources across participants. Asynchronous updates and delay-backpropagation techniques help mitigate communication delays and reduce the impact of stale gradients. We have also introduced a unique compression method utilizing quantization in both the model and gradient parameters, as well as a resource-aware learning rate adjustment that accommodates participants' varying abilities. Furthermore, we have proposed an innovative bi-directional compression approach that allows for inter-parameter compression. Our RC-FedOnline algorithm is the first to address the issue of unequal resource allocation in distributed learning settings effectively. Moreover, it surpasses existing asynchronous and compression-based models, including counterfactual aggregation, by establishing an optimal balance between efficiency and accuracy. Reducing photoabsorption in thin silicon films is essential to increase the overall photoconductivity of the structure. Although improved absorption can be achieved with nanostructured films, these structures also increase photoconductivity. To resolve this, we propose and evaluate numerically a novel configuration consisting of a thin silicon film paired with a 3D photonic band gap reflector made from silicon instead of metal. Compared to a similar system using a metal reflector, our configuration results in significantly enhanced absorption across a broader wavelength range, including the solar spectrum. Additionally, the improved absorption was attributed to the enhanced scattering of light within the silicon reflector, a phenomenon not observed when using a metal reflector. Notably, our numerical findings indicate that the enhanced absorption is accompanied by reduced light penetration depth, highlighting the complex interplay between absorption and light propagation within the structure. Nevertheless, the improved absorption can be refined through further optimization, focusing on enhancing the light's penetration depth. This can be achieved by refining the design of the photonic band gap reflector to produce more forward-scattered light, which would increase the light's interaction with the thin silicon film and boost absorption. Our study provides valuable insights for improving absorption in thin silicon films, especially in the context of solar cells and photodetectors. This knowledge can be adapted to other thin-layer semiconductor materials to enhance optical processing, sensing, or electrical conversion within thin films. Furthermore, we explored the potential for self-assembly techniques to produce the nanostructured silicon reflectors, which could significantly lower production costs. Finally, we evaluated the efficacy of surface roughening as a simplified method for achieving 3D structure equivalent using a thin silicon film and found it to be ineffective, resulting in significantly reduced absorption. Consequently, the improved structure identified in this study may serve as an efficient solar cell architecture, and its application in the manufacturing of solar cells and other thin silicon devices could lead to a significant breakthrough. The extensive numerical data obtained in this study are available online, and we expect that the information could be leveraged to design and fabricate similar architectures using other semiconductor materials. Additionally, the computational framework employed in this theoretical research can be adapted to investigate various other nanostructured systems and their potential applications in the manufacturing of solar cells, optical sensing, and electrical conversion. We introduce a new class of high dimensional extenders, derived from covered families of subsets. Leveraging the existing concept of base of covered families, we establish a corresponding notion, applicable to high dimensional reductive groups and demonstrating an analogy with its one-dimensional counterpart, the matrix multiplication property. Building upon this framework, we derive new classes of simple groups, using covered families to generate endoscopic data, thereby enabling the construction of stable average census data. Additionally, we exploit the properties of these high dimensional extenders to gain insight into covered families themselves, via a novel infinite dimensional analogue of the Bruck-Ulam theorem. Furthermore, we establish an explicit example of a high dimensional extender with minimal complexity, characterized by a symmetric structure and a small entry condition in the matrix representation. This work contributes significantly to the ongoing efforts to construct stable forms of character varieties and generic representations of classical groups. Ultimately, these findings have the potential to facilitate the development of new techniques for construction of stable forms in moduli space contexts. The methods employed in this research comprise a combination of analytic and algebraic tools, drawing from fields like representation theory, endoscopy, mod p reduction and high dimensional expanders, offering a rich and diverse combination of approaches. A central outcome of this work is the establishment of an analogy between the problem of constructing stable forms in character varieties and the task of deriving useful properties from high dimensional expanders, an area where significant progress has previously been made. The distinction between these two problems lies in the fact that high dimensional expanders are primarily a topic of study within the field itself, as opposed to the case with covered families, where we are seeking applications of this concept. The existing literature on high dimensional expanders is primarily focused on obtaining explicit constructions of stable forms, using a variety of approaches, whereas our research offers a new perspective by leveraging covered families, an area where we are ultimately seeking to apply the properties of high dimensional expanders. The solution to the open problem we propose has the potential to be pivotal in the field of high dimensional expanders, potentially enabling new constructions and advancements. Ultimately, SSNE's validity is established through a thorough experimental analysis that demonstrates its adaptability to sparse networks and its ability to generate node representations that are sensitive to network structure, thus making SSNE a more practical solution for prediction tasks on such networks. The research also highlights key factors of network density required for SSNE's model to produce accurate predictions. This cell design allows for easy birefringence alignment and incorporates an optical window for accessible laser interaction. This allows the extraction of a million-fold increase in signal phase, up to 40 rad, when paired with a clock signal. By integrating the cell with an optical cavity, we have achieved a level of precision, measured as the square root of the signal phase, approaching the quantum limit. Preemptive wildfire detection depends heavily on spatial and temporal analysis of
visible and infrared imagery, although combining these modalities is challenging due
to differences in resolution and modality mismatch. Traditional methods rely on a
structured optical model, which often fails to account for noise and assumes
visible-infrared modality correlations that don't always exist. This study presents
a novel, data-driven approach called FIRe-GAN that synthesizes visible-infrared
imagery using generative adversarial networks. Evaluated on real-world wildfires
imaged by advanced cameras, FIRe-GAN outperforms existing methods by significant
means, also proving adaptable to new datasets with minimal domain adaptation. 
With its potential for scalable deployment, FIRe-GAN makes feasible the automatic
fusion of visible-infrared imagery in real-time surveillance systems, enabling
early and automated wildfire detection. An accompanying software package is
available under an open-source MIT license at https://github.com/sseem517/FIRe-GAN.

In the model we are about to introduce, compartments represent distinct groups of individuals, transitioning over time as individuals move between them. For COVID-19, we specifically create a model with five categories: those yet to be infected, those infected but unaffected, those infected and showing symptoms, those hospitalized and recovering, and those who have survived the illness. Each category is associated with a stochastic rate at which individuals transition between them.

This type of model is known as an irreversible continuous-time Markov chain. Because exact calculations for such models are generally impossible, we utilize two complementary techniques to estimate probabilities. One technique involves renormalization to yield an approximate, yet simpler model. The other technique leverages Stein's Factorization Theorem and the Feynman-Kac Formula to derive an intuitive expression for unconditioned probabilities.

The model we've developed seeks to account for the following factors: (a) the overall infection rate, influenced by factors such as social distancing and population density; (b) the conversion rate of asymptomatic to symptomatic individuals; (c) the proportion of symptomatic cases that require hospitalization; (d) the case fatality risk; and (e) the recovery rate of patients. Each parameter can be expressed in terms of time scales. Furthermore, we also determine the conditional probabilities of transitioning between specific states within a fixed timeframe and apply this model to analyze the outcomes of governmental policies using simulated scenarios. Finally, we approximate the model's unconditioned probabilities and derive a concise formula that expresses the overall infection rate as a function of social distancing and population density. The model is then used to predict the outcomes of governmental policies in a city with 1 million inhabitants located in the southern United States. The model's predictions are also compared to the actual COVID-19 outbreak in that city. Lastly, we propose a set of data that researchers can use to model COVID-19 infections in any location, given that they have access to reliable information about local demographics, healthcare infrastructure, and the proportion of individuals who engage in social distancing. The aim of this system is to maintain a desired, yet variable, velocity while preventing stick-slip motion, but the introduction of Coulomb friction and non-zero stiffness in the model leads to a solution set for the dynamic system that is non-continuous and unbounded. The system's ability to converge and the characteristics of the resulting solution set are therefore areas of concern. The presence of an infinite number of solutions where convergence is possible raises additional issues, as the system's performance is heavily dependent on the specific force applied in each instance. A thorough analysis of the system's behavior is therefore necessary to determine if convergence is achievable and under what conditions. The resulting set of convergence points would provide valuable insights into the system's behavior and help to determine the feasibility of achieving a smooth, continuous motion using the PPF control method. The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a source and a Fuchsian hypergeometric differential equation. Notably, the hypergeometric equation exhibits a singular limit case where the residue of the source vanishes. Moreover, despite the reducible nature of the equation, its solution exhibits independence from a critical parameter in the unfolding process. These exceptional properties suggest the double confluent Heun equation's solution possesses particular symmetry properties, which are further explored in this paper. Building on the generalized symmetric folding concept, we discuss the solution's behavior in the singular limit and provide an extension of the earlier findings. Additionally, we present an extension of a known identity involving the hypergeometric differential equation, its associated monodromy matrix, and the hypergeometric function itself. Lastly, we provide an updated version of a representation formula for the hypergeometric function in terms of Bessel functions. The proposed updates on the hypergeometric equation's solution properties align with the recent general unfolding framework established in \cite{Miller:2017}: they imply the solution can be expressed as a product of two special functions, which can be further factorized into two confluent hypergeometric functions, each corresponding to the equation's constituent parts. The solution's properties are then studied further in the context of the generalized symmetric folding framework in \cite{fuchsianframework}. The framework allows for an extension into higher-dimensional spaces, as shown in \cite{higherdimensionalextension}. This study addresses matrix estimation issues involving a single column rank deficiency. Initially, we investigate the theoretical limitations of estimating low-rank matrices under constrained singular value distributions and additive error noise. These limitations are then applied to the related problem of matrix denoising. Furthermore, we consider the scenario of matrix estimation with heterogeneous noise, addressing both the case where noise variances belong to a specified set of finite measure and the case where variances decrease as a polynomial of the order $1/\rho^a$ with $a$ between 0 and 1. We demonstrate that under polynomially decreasing variances, a fundamental limit on the estimation error exists and can be realized with a suitable selection method for matrix columns. This is achieved by using a modified version of the canonical certificate method, a technique that was initially proposed in the context of homogeneous noise by Roussel et al. (2021). Our findings on matrix estimation with heterogeneous noise are further extended to the related problem of semi-definite programming with heterogeneous data. A novel method for rank-one regression analysis under heterogeneous noise is also presented, addressing the challenge of estimating linear regression parameters in the presence of heterogeneous residuals resulting from non-symmetric linear model covariance. This method, which outperforms the symmetrically-weighted estimator in the case of uniformly distributed noise, involves a bandwidth selection procedure that is free of any model-related parameters. Our theoretical findings are also grounded in a collection of empirical performance evaluations that highlight the method's practical efficiency.
