This paper adapts the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture to address the Question-Answering (QA) task. It integrates elements from a Denoising Prompt Reconstruction (DPR) retriever and a Generative model based on a pre-trained T5 big language model. Notably, existing QA benchmarks, such as the SQuAD dataset, were not pre-trained on the specific text to which the models were later exposed. Consequently, this work innovates by introducing an end-to-end QA model that seamlessly integrates a memory efficient dense retrieval system and seamlessly combines it with a Generative model to assemble a fully equipped SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) machine.

To begin, this paper's research extends existing prompt tuning methods by applying it to the entire RAG architecture, incorporating suggestions from AutoGL to map tokens to embeddings and utilizing prompt vector generation via prompt-mers. It also introduces negative prompt tuning as a vector gradient regularization technique which greatly enhances the retriever's ability to accurately select relevant information from a large database and substantially lowers the computational cost involved.

Our approach was evaluated on six diverse datasets, showcasing prompt based RAG's exceptional adaptability and versatility. It successfully achieved a range of improvements including significant enhancements to performance, such as increasing Demovire's performance on the STS-AQ dataset by 2.2 points, and extending its capabilities to fully unsupervised scenarios, such as with the natural questions dataset where human annotated labels are non-existent. Furthermore, this work's adaptable and efficient nature allows for rapid model fine tuning with minimal resources, such as time, money, and expertise. Our code has been made publicly available for other researchers to use. Online crowdsourcing platforms, including MTurk, have become essential tools for conducting linguistic research through participant recruitment, presenting tasks, and evaluating participant responses. Nevertheless, MTurk's worker pool is comprised of a mix of professional researchers and non-experts, making it a challenge to identify and engage only qualified participants, especially for time-sensitive studies. Our study aims to explore MTurk's qualification system and investigate the effectiveness of setting and managing demographic and skill-based qualifications to attract qualified crowdsourcers, using a pilot experiment inspired by a real-world MTurk-based linguistics study. Our key findings include (a) the impact of demonstration requirements on participant engagement, (b) the efficacy of skill qualifications in filtering out ineligible workers, and (c) the limitations of MTurk's qualification system and tips for MTurk researchers to increase the chances of engaging qualified crowdsourcers. Our work is expected to provide valuable insights for MTurk researchers to design successful studies, and we hope our tools and resources will aid other researchers in understanding MTurk's qualification system and facilitate the design of more effective MTurk studies. Ultimately, through MTurk-based research, researchers can gather richer, more informative data. But first, we must successfully recruit qualified crowdsourcers. Unfortunately, very little existing MTurk research has investigated this key challenge. Our study hopes to fill this knowledge gap and pave the way for future MTurk researchers to conduct superior crowdsourced linguistic research. This paper uses "crowdsourcer" to denote participants recruited to complete a specific task, and "worker" to denote MTurk account holders, to avoid confusion. Additionally, the terms "qualification" and "demographic information" refer to specific requirements set by MTurk researchers, and "skill qualification" and "demographic qualification" respectively refer to qualifications based on workers' alleged skills or demographics. Finally, the term "qualification task" denotes a series of tasks designed to evaluate participants' skills or demographics. Our investigation is grounded in a real-world MTurk-based study, in which participants recruited to complete sentence fusion tasks. Our primary objectives were (a) to explore the effectiveness of setting a demonstration qualification for engaging qualified crowdsourcers, and (b) to investigate the impact of skill qualifications on participant filtering. Ultimately, the study reveals key insights into the design of qualifications, and provides general tips and tools for MTurk researchers to design successful studies. Our focus is on text-text retrieval, specifically the text-clip retrieval (TCR) branch of text-vision, where incoming text and vision features from a particular location or scene are repeatedly evaluated against a large pre-trained text-vision model to find matches. Since current top-ranking methods are too slow for real-time retrieval from large datasets, we developed TS2-Net - a neuro-symbolic transformer architecture that efficiently performs token shifting and selection from embedded text and vision features. This is achieved through the interaction of two interconnected components: a visual attention-based shifting predictor, which determines the movement of tokens from text features, and a token selection operator, which performs hard selection based on a weighted average of two encoded text representations. Our experimental results show that TS2-Net outperforms other models in terms of real-time retrieval from large datasets of various sizes, while also surpassing the current state-of-the-art accuracy in text-clip retrieval. A comprehensive set of ablation studies confirm the significance of each model component. Furthermore, we introduce the 2D-MSRC dataset as a rigorous evaluation platform to assess the true real-time performance of TSNets under extreme scale. An open-source implementation of our method in PyTorch can be found at https://github.com/kemaloks/TS2-Net. This study introduces a novel approach to identify disturbances on power distribution networks by analyzing wireless measurements captured through neoteric technology. A novel deep learning model based on convolutional neural networks is suggested for interpreting the spatial and temporal aspects of interference. Additionally, a data-preprocessing technique is proposed to simplify interpretation of sensor data. The research further explores the use of ensemble learning methods for boosting the model's accuracy in predicting multiple types of interference occurring simultaneously. Evaluation using simulated data confirms the effectiveness of the proposed framework in pinpointing interferences from signal spectra. With an accuracy of nearly 85%, the proposed framework demonstrates a significant enhancement in classification performance for multiple labels compared to traditional optimization methods. Further analysis through sensitivity testing underscores the importance of spatial data in identifying interferences, as opposed to temporal data, highlighting the need for balanced sampling in the training dataset. The model's ability to accurately classify interference on power distribution networks was verified at the micro level. The proposed framework presents a promising solution to detecting disturbances on power distribution networks through shared wireless sensors, paving the way for possible automation in distribution systems. A non-trivial, locally usual measure algebra is able to support a countable, transitive set of real numbers with a well-defined translation structure. Measure algebras that are countable, finite, or ergodic with respect to a given group are inherently locally usual. A measure algebra that is ergodic with respect to a compact group can be expressed as the quotient of a compact abelian group's measure algebra under continuous Haar measurement only if it is finite. Measure algebras that are ergodic with respect to $R^infty$ can be expressed as the quotient of Haar measurement on a compact open subgroup only if they are finite. The quasi-ergodicity criterion also holds for locally usual, ergodic measure algebras with respect to $R^infty$. A new method of constructing flow-measure algebras has also been developed. Specifically, for any countable set of real numbers denoted as $[0,c]$, a flow-measure algebra has been constructed such that its associated radical is trivial, its ergodic measure algebras are finite, and its Haar measurement corresponds to the Haar measurement on the compact abelian group $K_{c+1}$, where $K_{c+1}$ is the one-point compactification of the Minkowski space. Finally, a locally usual, non-ergodic measure algebra has been constructed such that its ergodic measure algebras are finite. The conventional view of artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly inadequate, largely due to the significant advances made in the field. This has led to the emergence of the concept of Synthetic Intelligence (SI), which encompasses both theoretical and practical aspects of artificial intelligence. However, despite SI, genuine artificial intelligence that functions independently remains unattainable. This paper seeks to address this limitation by proposing the idea of Augmented Synthetic Intelligence (ASI), which combines elements of SI and Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Furthermore, ASI aims to bridge the gap between SI and AGI by incorporating augmentations that are not necessarily intelligent in nature. This concept serves as a theoretical framework for further evaluation and development. Additionally, ASI raises fundamental concerns that set it apart from traditional AI, ultimately framing the field as a distinctive area of study. This research marks the initial exploration of this unique and intriguing concept. Consequently, the present study seeks to offer a foundational understanding of ASI. Its potential applications and implications in fields like corporate and impact assessment are areas for further research and investigation. Finally, the study concludes by exploring the potential drawbacks or hazards associated with ASI and discusses ways to mitigate them. Key words: artificial intelligence, synthetic intelligence, augmented synthetic intelligence, agi, si, cognitive augmentations. Our research focuses on the collective behavior of a specific model that describes bosons interacting with fermions in an optical lattice, taking into account spin-orbit coupling and correlations. The ground state of this system is found to exhibit modulated superfluidity, and we study its thermal behavior using Bogoliubov theory. In doing so, we uncover various thermal phase transitions, and show that they can be observed under realistic experimental conditions. These results are expected to be experimentally verified in the near future. A notable development is the emergence of zero-temperature phase transitions between the original superfluid and the lattice-phased fermions, facilitated by the spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we identify new thermal phase transitions not found in systems without interactions between spin and orbit, including a twisted superfluid to twisted Bose condensate phase transition, and a twisted superfluid to gas phase transition, both of which occur as the system approaches its critical temperature. The research also reveals the presence of condensed particles even at temperatures above the critical point. A discussion of possible experimental realizations, including a development based on spin-orbit coupling made from p-band semiconductor microstructures, is provided in the text. Our goal in this study is to explore the characteristics of graphs that belong to type $[G,D]$ with respect to abelian groups $G$. Recent breakthroughs in research on Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory correspondences in lower dimensions have been explored using Type IIA theory with massive quanta in the bulk. Specifically, we have analyzed how conformal dimensions are influenced by a boundary theory's details in four specific scenarios: In the first scenario, we studied holographic fixed points of four-dimensional gauge theories with supersymmetry, finding a duality that extends beyond the Neveu-Schwarz sector. Our results also imply a universal lower bound on conformal dimensions. In the second scenario, we investigated fixed points of conformal gauge theories in three dimensions, using a novel spin connection to derive constraints on the boundary theory's Casimir effects. We found that these effects can encode the magnetic response of a boundary gauge theory. In the third scenario, we discovered a new solution in four-dimensional spacetime that represents a dual probe string interpretation. Our solution implies that conformal dimensions have a lower bound. In the fourth scenario, we have developed a new solution in three-dimensional spacetime that represents a dual probe string interpretation, using a non-trivial backround field that generates a confinement potential. Our results suggest that conformal dimensions are influenced by the boundary theory's details. We also discussed how these solutions can be related to known quantum field theories. We have explored gapless excitations on these boundaries using these new solutions. Our results provide novel insights into AdS/CFT correspondence in low dimensions. Future colliders relying on muons as beams and incorporating multiple TeV energy ranges will face a significant challenge in minimizing unwanted beam-beam effects, which are generated by the strong Coulomb interactions between these beams. Given that conventional techniques will not be sufficient to overcome these effects, which are driven by the inverse square of the beam momentum, innovative methods to reduce these interactions need to be developed. This, in turn, requires highly precise control over the muon and electron content in the beams, as well as very low levels of beam width and long-range correlations. Some novel approaches to reduce these unwanted effects include deliberately introducing excess negative charge along the beam path and utilizing new technologies to create "anti-beams" that can help cancel out the Coulomb interactions between the beams. These concepts are traced from their origins in past research to their potential application in future muon colliders, where they could help reduce beam-related effects by at least one order of magnitude, enabling these devices to meet the precise requirements needed to discover new physics at the TeV energy level. This includes the potential use of delibately created "anti-muon" beams to reduce Coulomb interactions between the beams. Note that the precise requirements of the future lepton-lepton colliders will lead to breakthroughs in various fields of accelerator physics and particle physics and make them the most precisely controlled particle accelerators ever constructed, ultimately enabling them to uncover new physics waiting to be discovered at the TeV energy level, particularly at muon colliders that have the potential to achieve a very high luminosity through the creation of precise muon-antimuon pairs using the Muon Collider Working Group's preferred muon ionization cooling technology. This, in turn, could enable the detection of new physics at the muon collider's energy ranges, potentially beyond the reach of the Large Hadron Collider. Some of the potential discoveries that could be made include the detection of the Higgs boson in the charged lepton channels, the search for right-handed neutrinos at high energies, the discovery of possible beyond the Standard Model behavior of the Z boson in certain processes and potentially resolving the anomalies at the LHC, the precise measurement of the mass of the W and Z bosons, the final precise measurement of the weak mixing angle, the precise measurement of the anomalous magnetic moments of the leptons and a direct, precise measurement of the properties of dark matter candidates. Encouraging neural networks to make more efficient use of resources by limiting the amount of data they process can be an effective way to tackle complex problems. However, existing methods that try to limit the sequence length in neural networks suffer from two key drawbacks. Firstly, they force models to skip over crucial data, which can negatively impact their performance for tasks that require sequential processing. Alternatively, they allow models to anticipate data ahead of time, which can compromise their fairness in tasks that rely on predictive accuracy. A new approach, based on optimization and flow models, has been proposed as a more effective way to manage neural network resources by controlling the amount of data used in processing, without disrupting the model's natural behavior. It takes advantage of an iterative transportation algorithm and leverages a novel objective that combines both sparse and predictive components. Experimental results show that it consistently produces more balanced and accurate models compared to existing methods. It also achieves better performance in tasks such as NLP, when compared with traditional neural network architectures. Furthermore, it shows great potential in tasks that require sequential processing, such as language modeling and machine translation. Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a fundamental aspect of their development processes. However, unit tests can become ineffective due to test smells, which compromise the quality of test code and potentially harm the system, leading to unintended consequences. Previous research has identified various test smells along with their potential impact on test success. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals provides vital insights into heart function, allowing for beat-by-beat diagnosis at a doctor's office or with remote health devices. Accurate IBIs depend on precise signal processing, but raw data typically contains noise and artifacts stemming from non-uniform sampling rates, DC shift, and lead-off signals. These imperfections necessitate beating template localization and noise filtering to extract reliable IBI data. Our research focuses on the latter, leveraging a Tiramisu model to transform IBIs from a sequential to an image-based format and facilitating faster, more accurate estimation. By transforming the problem into an image processing context, we can employ noise reduction techniques, such as frequency filtering and non-local means algorithms, to generate sharper, more reliable templates. In addition, our approach eliminates the need for explicit beat detection and can also be extended to processing unevenly sampled signals, making it an ideal method for remote monitoring and telehealth applications. Our experimental results indicate that this image-based method reduces average IBI estimation error to 0.48ms and achieves a fast processing speed of 2.07s for 200 beats. Moreover, the associated code has been released for the LEC 2020 LIA challenge. Our novel algorithm is expected to have a significant impact on the development of next-generation wearable devices, paving the way for seamless integration of heart monitoring into daily life and the human environment. We have developed a randomized SVD algorithm for tensors that requires an arbitrary number of passes. This method uses multi-way SVD decompositions of outer product factors to achieve a decomposition of the tensor into its factor matrices and corresponding singular value tensors. This approach is pass-sensitive, meaning the number of passes can be chosen adaptively based on the desired balance of memory and time efficiency, at the expense of a probabilistic tradeoff. For a specified failure probability, our randomized method reduces the expected computational cost and memory usage by a factor of $\log^2 k$ for $O(k^3/\log k)$ passes, where $k$ is the dimensionality of the tensor's largest mode. This makes our approach memory-efficient for large $k$ scenarios. By further reducing passes to $\sqrt{k}$, we incur a corresponding increase in computational overhead by a factor of $\log k$. This randomized method is an empirical approximation that leverages randomized tensor decompositions to achieve the desired balance of computational and memory tradeoffs. We provide the underlying theoretical guarantees for our algorithm. By experimental verification, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. However, real-world graphs are often marked by continuous changes, or additions, to their edges and vertices. This dynamic nature of graphs poses a major hurdle in the adoption of traditional graph embedding techniques. The success of these traditional methods is drastically reduced when direct static graph embeddings are utilized. In an effort to address this challenge, researchers have recently proposed dynamic graph embedding frameworks that take into consideration the evolution of graphs over time. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, a combined effort was made to integrate contact tracing services into the national tracing program in England, with the primary goal of slowing the virus's spread. Research has shown that local tracing initiatives can enhance the program's effectiveness, but the overall efficiency of the national program and the optimal mix of resources for these local efforts were yet unknown quantities. Using a Bayesian hierarchical model, we analyzed daily COVID-19 hospitalization data in England, dividing it into distinct episodes where the virus's growth was stagnant, accelerating, or declining. This analysis allowed us to compare the hospitalization rates in areas with and without local tracing initiatives. Our results indicate that the implementation of these local efforts slowed hospitalization growth in their regions by 16-28%, but did not affect areas without such programs. Although the findings of this study are generally encouraging, the present average regional efficiency of the national program during the study period was 24% when compared to models that only considered national contact recovery rates. Additionally, the present average national efficiency was 26%, representing a 12% improvement in program efficiency since the beginning of the pandemic. Furthermore, the study's results suggest that local tracing programs were more effective later in the pandemic, indicating a potential need to optimize the national program's resources, including targeting regions where the virus's growth is accelerating for more focused efforts. While the study's results are based on COVID-19 hospitalization data, the analysis's hierarchical model can be adapted to other fields using time series data that features distinct episodes of growth. In real-world settings, learning the optimal control policies for complex systems often proves challenging due to the difficulties associated with providing robots with a deep understanding of their objectives. To address this issue, we explore a novel approach in this paper: using a controller's actual behavior to uncover the underlying rewards and constraints that drive its decision-making process. We develop two novel methods, one constrained by both reward and constraints and one constrained solely by constraints, both aimed at learning the controller's target task parameters. Building upon a model-based method established in the literature, our research reveals that learning the constraints is inherently more difficult than learning the rewards and reveals a unique relationship between the two. Additionally, our constraint-learning algorithm offers several key advantages, including the ability to constrain learning within specific task domains and efficiently scale up by leveraging observations from multiple controllers. We validate the efficacy of our method using a simulated reaching task and provide evidence of its practical applicability through a comparison with a publicly available, reward-shaping algorithm. The methods presented in this study represent a crucial step towards a future framework that empowers controllers to self-learn their objectives. A vertex divider in a graph $G$ with respect to a given vertex $v$ is defined as an induced subgraph $H$ of $G$, formed by splitting $G$ into two parts $C_1$ and $C_2$, where $v$ belongs to $C_1$, ensuring that for any vertex in $C_2$, all paths to $v$ only go through $C_1$. This concept is utilized in treewidth computation through vertex branch and bound, where finding the vertex divider leading to maximum weight tree branch significantly influences the tree decomposition's weight. In fast treewidth algorithms, the number of vertex dividers with specific properties is a limiting factor, causing these algorithms to become exponential when the required number of dividers exceeds this limit. To overcome this constraint, we introduce new types of vertex dividers, referred to as $k$-shell and $(k, \delta)$-shortest-path vertex dividers, in an effort to reduce the need for these dividers within branch and bound algorithms. By experimenting with these new types of vertex dividers, we improve the upper bound on treewidth, demonstrating that our proposed approach is more efficient than standard treewidth algorithms. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical efficacy of our approach by applying it to the previously solvable but poorly performing instances of the Hamiltonian Path Problem, resulting in reduced search spaces and faster solution times. As an added benefit, we examine the frequency of required $(k, \delta)$-shortest-path vertex dividers in actual graphs, revealing that three such dividers is an infrequent requirement. This discovery allows us to implement an efficient search strategy for the Hamiltonian Path Problem that benefits from the properties of frequent vertex dividers, even in cases involving infrequent dividers. Overall, we examine the trade-offs between search performance based on the different types of vertex dividers, ultimately aiming to understand the average and worst-case requirements for these dividers within the Hamiltonian Path Problem and treewidth computation contexts. In addition to these experiments, we also validate the practical efficiency of our approach by applying it to the recently proposed NP-complete graph model, the Maximal Independent Vertex Cover Constrained Vertex Cover, in an effort to solve this problem efficiently. Finally, we briefly outline promising areas of future research related to the concepts presented. A corresponding project involving the implementation of the proposed approach has been shared at https://github.com/AIResearchGroup/Project-231.README.

We establish two distinct types of tunneling behavior, one resulting from Majorana zero modes and the other from generic zero-energy states. A non-local current injection method is introduced to differentiate between these states by analyzing a peak appearing in a conductance curve. This peak, denoted as the "zero-energy peak," is resistant to variations in gate voltage. However, upon injecting current non-locally, the peak exhibited by a Majorana zero mode through tunneling spectroscopy remains tied to the gap energy. Conversely, the peak associated with a generic zero-energy state lacks this correlation. Additionally, to enhance our approach, we propose incorporating a dissipative element into tunneling electrodes. This element generates a local bias altering the tunneling Hamiltonian and gives rise to a finite conductance even without an external voltage applied, a phenomenon referred to as Ohmic dissipation. A peak resulting from Majorana zero modes and Ohmic dissipation can be distinguished by analyzing their widths, as the latter results in a peak with an infinitely small width. To further establish the validity of our approach, we have performed numerical simulations of the tunneling behavior incorporating both bulk and edge fluctuations. A comprehensive study of the tunneling behavior employing non-local current injection and ohmic dissipation with resistive electrodes is presented. This approach has the potential to be adapted for scanning tunneling microscopy, making it a reliable experimental technique for establishing the existence of Majorana zero modes. Moreover, this method offers the added benefit of measuring the energy gap of the host material. A second-order phase transition was observed in systems exhibiting ohmic dissipation and bulk fluctuations. Conversely, systems with edge fluctuations exhibited the characteristics of a first-order phase transition as embodied by a sharp peak in the tunneling behavior. Our analytical models and numerical simulations provide the theoretical foundation for this research and can be used to inform future experimental setups. Moreover, these models have the added value of contributing to the understanding of the fundamental aspects of Majorana zero modes and ohmic dissipation. To facilitate future research, we have compiled essential knowledge into a concise textbook, which is presented in supplementary materials. The present study and associated analytical models and numerical simulations enable the establishment of the functional reliability of Majorana zero modes through tunneling spectroscopy with ohmic dissipation using resistive electrodes. This work also contributes significantly to the advancement of related theoretical models by establishing the distinguishing characteristics of Majorana zero modes and ohmic dissipation at a fundamental level. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different latitudes of the 2DEG flow in opposite directions due to distinct energy levels.  Despite this concept being widely suggested, experiments on gap introduction face significant challenges due to the need to manipulate moiré patterns at extremely precise lengths ($< 1$ nm).  A new approach is presented where the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene is explored as an alternative to the valley Hall effect.  It's demonstrated that the orbital Hall effect can be effectively observed in gapped graphene by introducing an 'orbital up-down asymmetry' by breaking the spatial inversion symmetry of the system, regardless of the absence of energy band asymmetry.  A realistic scenario involving the formation of Mott insulators from the stacking of two coplanar hexagonal layers is studied to illustrate the introduction of orbital up-down asymmetry.  It's found that the orbital Hall effect leads to the flow of an 'orbital current', positioned perpendicularly to the 2DEG and moiré pattern, which is proportional to both the orbital asymmetry and moiré occupation pattern, while being inversely related to the 2DEG resistance.  Notably, this 'orbital current' can be equivalent in magnitude to the valley Hall effect and is generated independently of the chemical potential, making it observable at any value without being hindered by certain specific regimes.  A proposed device, incorporating gapped graphene as a central component, is then designed to harvest and visualize the orbital Hall effect by creating a controlled circulation of current within a central hole, while the effect is also compared to the valley Hall effect in terms of magnitude and visibility, with the former being more controllable and the latter being more visible.  Ultimately, this research provides an all-encompassing view of the orbital up-down asymmetry and its effect, using it as a connecting link between the orbital Hall effect and the valley Hall effect, while also highlighting the unique substantial similarities and differences between these two effects at a deep level.  A new interpretation is presented where the orbital up-down asymmetry serves as a common foundation to explain both the orbital and valley Hall effects as related phenomena.  It's found that the orbital Hall effect can be considered a specific manifestation of the valley Hall effect, occurring when the orbital asymmetry is discretely divided into separate energy levels, with the effect's magnitude equivalent to that of the valley effect and controlled independently of the chemical potential. An reinforcement learning strategy, reinforcement contamination generation, is proposed and integrated into the contamination generation process. Two variants of this approach have been developed, involving offline and online training. The performance of this approach has been evaluated across seven datasets for GNN models, with the results demonstrating significant improvement over traditional contamination methods in terms of performance degradation. Ontologies, widely used across the AI and data science spectrum, often consist of hundreds of concepts. Researchers across various fields are interested in identifying relationships between these entities, both within and across ontologies. Although graphical visualization shows connections between related concepts, large ontologies can overwhelm the viewer with excessive information. To solve this problem, we present OntoPlot, an innovative visualization tool that effectively communicates associations within and between large ontologies. By labeling and coloring entities based on their relevance, OntoPlot provides an intuitive view. Furthermore, we introduce a new method for plotting ontologies hierarchically and discuss how this visual representation facilitates the discovery of new concepts within the context of semantic search. Using two extensive datasets derived from Wikipedia and Wikipedia descriptions, we evaluate the practical applications of OntoPlot and demonstrate its ability to aid concept and association discovery, as well as contribute to the development of new ontologies. The development of OntoPlot has inspired further research into plot-based visualizations and will be adapted into an interactive tool for exploring and analyzing ontologies. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN for an end-to-end automatic speech recognition system, addressing the challenge of limited in-domain training data. By leveraging specially designed inter-domain loss, the network's representation is pushed closer to that of a well-performing domain. Concurrently, CycleGAN minimizes the discrepancy in label distributions between the two domains, allowing the system to leverage additional, unlabeled data from a performance-oriented domain. Experimental evaluations on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal significant improvements, with sentence error rates reduced by 15%, 20%, and up to 25%, respectively, through the integration of inter-domain loss and CycleGAN. Furthermore, the findings confirm that using a cycle-consistent inter-domain loss is superior to using two separate domain-specific models. We publicly release our implementation at https://github.com/aliqiu/ssl-eespr.

As a result, two distinct components emerge in the directionally dependent thermal diffusion coefficient, specifically the rigid molecules' contribution and the flexible molecules' collective contribution based on their thermal motion. Notably, the flexible molecules' collective contribution exhibits a significant dependence on their thermal motion intensity and reaches nearly twice that of the rigid molecules' contribution. Furthermore, a model is developed to describe how the time-averaged thermal diffusion coefficient of the flexible molecules changes in relation to their average extendedness and temperature, thereby providing insight into the influence of flexible internal degrees of freedom on thermal diffusion. Specifically, the model reveals that the temperature-dependent thermal diffusion of flexible molecules is primarily controlled by their internal degrees of freedom. Moreover, the temperature at which the thermal diffusion of rigid and flexible molecules becomes equally distributed depends heavily on the level of extension and can be substantially lowered as the average extendedness increases. A critical assessment is also provided regarding the experimental detection of the thermal diffusion of internal degrees of freedom within flexible molecules. Ultimately, the findings demonstrate that the thermal diffusion of internal degrees of freedom within flexible molecules constitutes a distinct and significant phenomenon that can provide valuable light on the underlying processes driving self-diffusion in dense systems due to their inherent link in dense conditions, especially in cases where the thermal diffusion of rigid molecules tends to zero. A main limiting factor of the model is also identified. The research further explores novel thermal engineering techniques that leverage the thermal motion of flexible molecules to produce targeted temperature distributions. Specifically, the findings demonstrate that heat can be naturally directed from cooler areas to warmer areas within a mixture of thermally diffusing rigid and flexible molecules, thereby potentially opening up new avenues for refrigeration applications. Moreover, the experimental detection of the thermal motion of flexible molecules and the influence of their thermal motion intensity on the Soret effect are extensively discussed. Ultimately, the current understanding of the thermal motion of flexible molecules is summarized and various promising research directions in this field are considered. This study presents an approach to reduce false positives in domain adaptive pedestrian detection by employing an unsupervised method that removes unnecessary detection boxes from candidate lists. A novel metric, calculated through domain adaptation, enables differentiation between positive and negative boxes. To maintain a balanced ratio of positive to negative boxes, the approach involves adjusting the metric by optimizing a simplified version of the metric, resulting in the creation of an unsupervised ranking system. Experimental data shows that box re-ranking significantly reduces false positives and improves detection accuracy, with performance boosted by at least 3.96% by combining it with domain adaptive methods. Additionally, box re-ranking enables the transfer of models trained on large datasets to smaller datasets with minimal positive annotations. With the introduction of box re-ranking, we establish a new state-of-the-art performance on the Citypersons benchmark. The code for box re-ranking is available in the open-source toolkit FairDetections, which provides a unified framework for domain adaptation and error mitigation in object detection.

The generation of synthetic music through A.G. Munger's algorithm, initially published in 1968, is examined in this study. This algorithm represents the earliest documented example of a generative music model. This study aims to enhance the algorithm's output by first increasing the dimensionality of its output from a single line of staff to a four-channel audio file. This is accomplished using a four-layered generative adversarial network consisting of a residual block, U-net architecture structure, and two-layered transposition inversion. Following the improvement of the algorithm's output, the quality of its results is evaluated using a listening test. Additionally, the study explores various combinations of audio front-ends in order to optimize the algorithm's output. It does this by comparing audio representations produced by the Helmholtz space, spectrogram, and deep learning model named VGGish. Listenability and audio quality scores from a listening test are used to evaluate and compare the different combinations. Furthermore, the study applies an audio enhancement model to improve the quality of the algorithm's results, and the effectiveness of this enhancement is also evaluated through a listening test. Finally, a comprehensive study of the algorithm's results is conducted, enabling researchers to explore the potential outcomes of performing exhaustive searches using generative models like A.G. Munger's algorithm. This study includes insights into various artistic applications of the algorithm, in addition to the creation of novel musical patterns. The generation of synthetic music through the algorithm resulting in pleasing outcomes indicates its robustness and reliability. Notably, it outperforms models with more recent architectures in various generative music applications. Consequently, the study provides valuable insights and suggestions for developing generative music models on large-scale musical representations. One such representation is VGGish, which is used in this study. Listenability and audio quality scores from the listening test reveal that combinations produced using the Helmholtz space and VGGish have superior quality and are more listenable in comparison to those produced using the spectrogram. Consequently, the study recommends using the Helmholtz space and VGGish in future generative music models requiring large-scale musical front-ends. Moreover, the study provides insights and suggestions for developing enhanced audio quality and is not limited to applications in generative music models. To incorporate syntax into neural machine translation (NMT), we propose an innovative method that builds upon existing decoding algorithms. This approach includes syntax-aware connections between sentences translated together. Specifically, we enhance the top-down tree structured decoding algorithm with new links that utilize parser predictions, resulting in a combined model that optimizes both sentence translations and syntax. In comparison to bottom-up decoding, our syntax-based links have access to complete target syntax, while in comparison to top-down decoding, our model has reduced memory requirements. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using state-of-the-art open-source NMT libraries and a large English-Chinese language pair, yielding a consistent improvement in translation accuracy and overall system efficiency. Moreover, we provide detailed analysis of our method's impact on various factors, including target sentence length, syntax complexity, and token vocabulary size. Finally, we show that our decoding algorithm can also improve neural parser accuracy when used alone. The implementation of our syntax-based NMT model is now available as an optional extension to the MARIAN-NMT system, providing a useful additional feature. These circuits, operating on initial states in a specific form, utilize a limited number of quantum gates, mostly by a random selection of Pauli-X gates, coupled with random rotations around the x-axis via Rx(t) gates, and are found to be remarkably effective at approximating expectations associated with observables that are also low-depth preparable. This specificity in observation measurement does not hinder the method's general applicability as we demonstrate it. Furthermore, our results show that expecting results from these circuits, operated on initial states prepared in thermal states and using a certain depth of gates (independent of the system size or number of qubits), to be accurate to the nth power, and we relate this to the no-cloning theorem. Moreover, we discovered that applying a particular sequence of Rx(t) gates, with angles that are multiples of pi, to a pure state results in a product state, and we extend this to entire quantum circuits. These findings are the foundation of a new approach for quantum tomography, utilizing a very limited number of measurements to determine the density matrix of a quantum state. We found that applying a very short, depth-2 circuit to a thermal state prepares a state that, when used in a particular measurement, releases a set of information that's necessary and sufficient for assessing the state's density matrix. This approach is found to be more efficient and effective than using other methods, especially for large systems and numerous qubits. Finally, we show that applying a very shallow circuit to a thermal state, and taking the average of certain expectations related to a particular observable, gives us information that's necessary and sufficient for assessing the state's probability distribution. This approach is found to be more efficient and effective than using other methods, and is especially useful for a wide range of scenarios. These findings are very significant, and open up new avenues for accurately understanding and characterizing quantum systems experimentally. Developing lightweight multilingual translation models using quantization and knowledge distillation has shown promise in reducing the computational burden. Given the existing scarcity of multilingual translation data, it is particularly crucial to explore methods for adapting such models to low-resource languages. In this study, we first assess the impact of training duration on the performance of quantized models, revealing that they can achieve state-of-the-art results in a relatively short time with large translation datasets. Additionally, we improve the existing framework by which a teacher model is compressed into a smaller model through knowledge distillation, leading to a subsequent increase in the survival rate of well-performing student models. Notably, the top-performing models among the distilled group consistently outperform their teacher model and other non-distilled candidates, even when trained for a short period. Ultimately, we utilize the improved knowledge distillation method to propose a two-stage compression process, combining it with dataset augmentation to achieve state-of-the-art results on a set of 8 low-resource languages from the MMTN corpus, yielding a significant 4.75 BLEU points improvement over the teacher model and surpassing the best previous results on languages like Vietnamese and Persian. Notably, the resulting models from this process exhibit increased stability, allowing them to translate correctly even with omitted input sentences, whereas the base teacher model and other non-performing students demonstrate such robustness only when translating up to 10 words beyond the input sequence. Ultimately, the proposed method achieves a level of translation accuracy comparable to the existing state-of-the-art models after being trained for a mere 1 hour, thereby accelerating the compression process by two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the proposed method allows for translation without missing context on languages like Hindi, Urdu, and Chinese when the input sentences exceed 20 words, and without sentence fragmentation on languages like Japanese and Arabic, thereby ensuring translation consistency. Our project's source code is publicly available for review at this link: https://github.com/joshkap/condenser. What's more, the compressed models from this study are currently being used in a production environment. Following a review of the study's findings and code, it is suggested that the application of condensing techniques could potentially expand the reach of language models like BERT and XLM to languages speaking native speakers who rely on machine translation in their daily lives. In the future, it is anticipated that the proposed method could potentially enable zero-data model compression, thereby paving the way for machine translation to become a seamless component of languages speaking native speakers' toolsets. Developing image descriptive models capable of producing high-quality, user-specified outputs has been a long-standing challenge. To tackle this issue, researchers proposed fine-tuning pre-trained visual models using datasets like Conceptual Captions. However, pre-trained models often produce outputs with inaccurately assigned grades and fail to meet specific description requirements. To overcome these limitations, we introduce CC-PMT, a novel approach that leverages prompt-based magic tricks to refine image descriptive models. By utilizing prompt magic tricks to adjust the visual focus, we can mitigate the issues associated with inaccurate output grades. Furthermore, we can engage users in the image descriptive process through controllable image description. Our results demonstrate the superiority of CC-PMT over existing methods, and its effectiveness in making prompt-based magic tricks applicable to image descriptive models. CC-PMT is now publicly available on this GitHub link.  https://github.com/zhouhug/CC-PMT.  This work adopts a different strategy from the original mirokens' work on prompt-based magic tricks, as explored in https://github.com/mirokens/pmt.  We also incorporate some critical adjustments from the original CC model as noted in https://github.com/jayelrazz/cc.  The major difference between our work and these references lies in research goal, methodology, and application.  We aim to refine image descriptive models with finer controls and more accurate outputs, whereas the original techniques focus on either generating magic prompts or pre-trained visual models.  To achieve our objective, we integrate prompt-based magic tricks into the image descriptive process, thereby advancing the existing techniques for data-driven image descriptive models.  Our findings have been experimentally validated, and we expect the future research on prompt-based magic tricks to build upon our work by controllably refining other data-driven models, particularly those applied in different computer vision tasks.  We hope the results of this study can pave the way for future research in this area.  To facilitate this, we have made CC-PMT's code and data available for the research community, thereby promoting further development of this technique and ultimately benefiting the LS MiraNet community. We propose a new set of states, the hyperangular Hoermander weight states, to effectively tackle the challenge of identifying separable states in a quantum system. Our approach not only offers a reliable method to separate atypical states but also provides valuable geometric insights into the distribution of separable states within the entire Hilbert space. In addition, this approach has impressive efficiency and can handle large-scale systems with substantial dimensions. We have successfully applied this method to the quantum systems consisting of multiple qubits or isotropic spin systems. Our results reveal that the Hoermander weight states can accurately capture the properties of state distributions especially in low-dimensional systems. However, as the system dimension increases, the Hoermander weight states become less effective in distinguishing separable states. Nevertheless, the areas where these states dominate have significant practical implications as they constitute a large subset of separable states with substantial volume. Our findings also suggest that the separability problem can be attributed to the combined effects of local entanglement and state regularity. Furthermore, the Hoermander weight states can be generalised to other forms of quantum state distribution such as the Wigner function and Weyl system. Our study paves the way for the creation of a machine learning model trained on hyperangular Hoermander weight state data, which may lead to the development of a fully autonomous algorithm for determining separable states in quantum systems. Such a model has the potential to be applied not only to systems described by the Hoermander weight states but also to any low-dimensional quantum system. Our approach has been further validated by verifying that the separable states identified as entropy regularized Hoermander weight states outperform the previously best-known algorithm, the sum of negative entropy method in terms of performance and volume. In recent years, the deployment of WiFi access points in residential homes has been greatly increased. As a result, the existing WiFi standard has been upgraded with new tools, including the IEEE 802.11k/v add-ons, which provide enhanced network performance by enabling new functionality: 11k facilitates backhaul link selection, while 11v controls device associations. Recently proposed techniques, such as the 11k/v hybrid approach, use these tools to optimize WiFi networks by adjusting backhaul links and device associations simultaneously. Notably, the 11k method excises poor performing extenders, while the 11v method associates devices with the most suitable access points and backhaul links. Both methods show promising results, but the 11v approach tends to overwhelm the network with association requests, which need to be prevented. To prevent this limitation, we suggest a new tool: Channel load conscious AP / Extender selection using IEEE 802.11k. This method selects the most suitable access points and backhaul links for device association by considering the available WiFi channels. Moreover, we upgrade this technique to prevent selecting isolated extenders by introducing a new metric: the isolation metric. Notably, the performance of this technique exceeds that of the 11k method in terms of data rate, while yielding results comparable to the 11v approach. Furthermore, this technique surpasses recent ones by preventing the network from 11v association overload and exceeding the 11v performance while doing so. Finally, this technique boasts a level of simplicity that allows it to be executed via a simple online/offline method, making it suitable for real-world WiFi network applications. Such a technique could be deployed as a lightweight WiFi access point option to provide enhanced network performance, particularly in situations where this performance impacts video streaming quality. A possible business model for this technique could be to offer it as an additional feature to WiFi routers sold in the market. Notably, the performance of this technique might decline in situations where WiFi networks are used for applications other than video streaming, which could in turn reduce the network performance beyond what is observed with the 11v approach. Thus, the execution method of this technique should be carefully considered depending on the application of WiFi networks.
